I

temal Affairs) moved that the House go into committee to consider the following proposed resolution:
Resolved, by the	Hduse of Commons,-
That it is expedient that Parliament do approve of the Convention and Protocol between His Majesty, in respect of the Dominion of Canada, and the United States of America, for regulating the level of the Lake of the Woods, and of identical letters of reference submitting to the International Joint Commission certain questions as to the regulation of the levels of Rainy Lake and other upper waters, laid upon the table of the House on Thursday, the 26th of February, 1925t which was signed at Washington on the twenty-fourth day of February, one thousand nine hundred and twenty-five, and which was signed on behalf of His Majesty in respect of Canada by the plenipotentiary therein named, and that this House do approve of the same.
Motion agreed to, and the House went into committee thereon, Mr. Gordon in the chair.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
maintopic: CANADA-UNITED STATES CONVENTION LAKE OF THE WOODS AND RAINY LAKE LEVELS
speechtext: I made some comments on this matter the other day when it was first introduced. I would like the government to explain what alterations have been made; why the protocol at the end; and generally what has been the cause of the many years of delay that have occurred, holding the matter unsettled until this time.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
maintopic: CANADA-UNITED STATES CONVENTION LAKE OF THE WOODS AND RAINY LAKE LEVELS
speechtext:
The matter is settled on the identical lines proposed by an order in council passed by the government of my right hon. friend (Mr. Meighen) in 1921.	The delay since that date was
largely occasioned by the action of the state of Minnesota, who were raising objections of one kind and another, principally urging the objection that it would be well to include Rainy lake and the upper lake levels, and that matter might be settled. We have contended, I think in line with the action of the former government, that the lake of the Woods question be settled first and that, as is provided before in the treaty, the matter of the upper lake levels be a matter of inquiry before the commission. Some attempt was made at one time to ask us to bind ourselves to accept the finding of the commission. My right hon. friend will notice that that has not been done. It is identical, without a change in any particular, so far as I am aware, with the arrangement that was proposed for the consummation of a treaty under the order in council of 1921. The delay was occasioned, as I stated before, by the action of representatives of the state of Minnesota, but they finally agreed to the treaty as it was presented, and it was ratified by congress. It remains for our ratification to put it into effect.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
maintopic: CANADA-UNITED STATES CONVENTION LAKE OF THE WOODS AND RAINY LAKE LEVELS
speechtext:
I understand, then, that
Governor Preus' contentions have been abandoned in so far as they conflict with the original lines of settlement?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
maintopic: CANADA-UNITED STATES CONVENTION LAKE OF THE WOODS AND RAINY LAKE LEVELS
speechtext: Yes.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
maintopic: CANADA-UNITED STATES CONVENTION LAKE OF THE WOODS AND RAINY LAKE LEVELS
speechtext:
I also understand that
the question of the upper lakes remains just where it always was, a subject for submission to the International Joint Commission without any commitment at all whether we accept or whether they accept. If I remember correctly, Governor Preus and Mr. Backus both were insistent upon the land owners affected in the lower lake regions sharing in some of the damages which would result from the upper lake control. This is one of the contentions, then, that have been abandoned by Governor Preus and the state of Minnesota?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
maintopic: CANADA-UNITED STATES CONVENTION LAKE OF THE WOODS AND RAINY LAKE LEVELS
speechtext:
Governor
Preus never pressed that point with us. What he did press with respect to damage was that there should be an arrangement as regards damage in the upper lakes. The difficulty was that he was trying to get a commitment of the governments to compensation for such damages as might accrue in the upper lakes after the finding of the commission. I am not sure whether that contention was put forward prior to 1922 or not, but the whole difficulty was the question of the upper lakes and the damages resulting there. My right hon. friend will remember that Mr. Backus was very heavily interested in the upper lakes as regards his own property, and it was really the question of the upper Lakes which delayed the whole thing. We would not agree, stating that we stood on the former ground; that we would not accept in advance the finding of the commission, but that we would let the matter go before the commission and abide by the result of that commission and the decision arrived at by the government.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
maintopic: CANADA-UNITED STATES CONVENTION LAKE OF THE WOODS AND RAINY LAKE LEVELS
speechtext:
There is really nothing
at variance with the original finding of the royal commission and the order in council authorizing the execution of the treaty in pursuance thereof?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
maintopic: CANADA-UNITED STATES CONVENTION LAKE OF THE WOODS AND RAINY LAKE LEVELS
speechtext: No.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
maintopic: CANADA-UNITED STATES CONVENTION LAKE OF THE WOODS AND RAINY LAKE LEVELS
speechtext:
I congratulate the government on adhering loyally to the wise lines laid down by their predecessors in this case.
Resolution reported.

stagedirection
speechtext:
Hon. H. S. BELAND (Minister of Soldiers' Civil Re-establishment) moved that the House go into committee on Bill No. 70, to amend the Pension Act.
Motion agreed to and the House went into committee, Mr. Gordon in the chair.
On section 1-Disabilities in respect of which pensions claimed.

I think the minister was
asked whether this new clause is the same as the clause which was introduced in the bill of last year?

speakerposition: Minister of Soldiers' Civil Re-establishment; Minister presiding over the Department of Health
speechtext:
This is a new provision.
The reason for it is to make the clause clearer. In some cases the disability which is pensionable makes its appearance one, two or three years after discharge, although it can be related to an injury or a disease that was incurred during service. The change is made in order to make it clearer that if the injury or disease was incurred during service, the disability which is related to it, though it might make its appearance long after discharge, would be pensionable. If my hon. friend will read the amendment-

I have read it. I will be
glad if the minister will give us an example of how the pension can be different under the new clause from what it was under the old. I cannot see how the new clause is capable of any different interpretation.

speakerposition: Minister of Soldiers' Civil Re-establishment; Minister presiding over the Department of Health
speechtext:
It has been so claimed
by the Board of Pension Commissioners, that if a strict interpretation of the clause is adhered to, some cases may arise in which the pension will not be awarded, whilst with the present amendment it will be perfectly clear that the injury or disease resulting in disability will make the disability pensionable when they are related to each other. I think myself the clause is clearer as it reads now. It will do away with any possibility of doubt, and that is the only object they have in view.

If the minister would
point out to the committee the different changes between the present bill and the bill of last year, that would facilitate matters.

speakerposition: Minister of Soldiers' Civil Re-establishment; Minister presiding over the Department of Health
speechtext:
My intention was to do
that, and I shall be glad to comply with my IMr. Mackenzie King.]
hon. frend's request, as the several clauses are called. The most important clauses were submitted to the House last year.

Has the minister
any idea of the number of cases in which pensions have been refused through a strict interpretation of the act?

speakerposition: Minister of Soldiers' Civil Re-establishment; Minister presiding over the Department of Health
speechtext:
I have no particular case
in mind at the present time, but had I given any thought to that question I might have been able to cite some instances in which such a situation might arise. If my hon. friend would apply his acumen to the clause as it is now amended and to the section as it previously stood he would see that in the present case the language is clearer and that there is no possibility of misinterpretation. Disability might make its appearance two or three years after discharge and be related to service overseas although such disability was not apparent at the date of discharge. As the clause now reads it provides that if the injury or disease resulting in disability was incurred during military service then the disability is pensionable. That suggestion was made by the board to render the section clearer.	Though they
agreed	that they	had not	interpreted itdifferently so far, they pointed out that the strict interpretation of the act as it stood before	might lead in some	cases to	therefusal	of pension	when the	disability	had
made its appearance long after discharge.

The amendment to section 1 does not go far enough; there are a large number of oases which it does not cover at all. Hundreds of men to-day, as the minister no doubt knows, are not one hundred per cent efficient, and this inefficiency is beyond any question traceable	to service	overseas.	A
great many men after their return worked a month or even a year or two and then found themselves disabled so far as any efficiency for civil pursuits was concerned, and under section 1 as now amended a large number of these cases will be barred out. Indeed, there are men whose disability arose from their war service who were not taken care of under the section as it originally stood and who even now will be left out of consideration. There should be a much more liberal interpretation of the intention of the clause. I know of a soldier who died in Winnipeg a short time ago to whom a pension had been refused, although he had served four years in the war, and his people had not enough money to bring him home for burial in Toronto in my own constituency. This man's sickness developed after the war, but there was no doubt whatever

Pension Act
that it was due to his service overseas. Such men are dying in thousands; every month there are hundreds of deaths occurring among those returned men who have been denied proper consideration through an illiberal interpretation of the act. The estimates for this department are five million less than a year ago. These men will not live forever; and I think that the time has come now for more generous treatment of our veterans. These men are getting up in years and they are unable to work 365 days in the year; and they have their families to keep. There are some of our Canadians as well, men who were brought up in this country, who went overseas early in the war, in their anxiety to get into active service, and joined the British forces, and now they are unable to get any pension, either from the British government or from the government of Canada and do not come under any existing legislation.

Did I understand the hon.
gentleman to say that, there were Canadians by birth who enlisted in the British forces and who did not get any pension?

Yes, I have in mind at the moment particularly the case of Colonel Young, of Kingston, who is well known to the hon. gentleman, I have no doubt. That soldier went and enlisted in the British forces, and when he applied for a pension he could not get it. Those of our veterans who are unable to get any consideration when in distress are now obliged to apply to the cities for relief. There occurs to my mind at the moment one case, a soldier named Taylor, in which I had some correspondence with the minister: a pension was refused this man who lives in the riding of my hon. friend from South Toronto (Mr. Sheard). He has been writing to the board for months without any satisfaction and was receiving assistance through the city. The authorities claim that his sickness was not due to service overseas. With all due respect to the minister, I do think that there should be some broad rule to cover all these cases. When application is made to the minister he says he can do nothing that is not laid down by the act; and after a lot of time is spent in correspondence with the board they take the same attitude. The result is that the city has to come to the relief of these men. The amendment to the act, I repeat, does not go far enough.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext:
Can the minister tell us
who drafted the clause as it stands? Was it drafted in the Justice department?
181*

speakerposition: Minister of Soldiers' Civil Re-establishment; Minister presiding over the Department of Health
speechtext:
I think it was submitted
by the secretary of the board.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext:
I prefer the drafting in
the old clause; it is simpler and at the same time more perspicuous. I am doubtful as to the wisdom of leaving out the words "attributable to." According to the present wording of the clause, the pension is payable if the injury or disease or aggravation thereof resulting in disability "was incurred during such military service." The old wording was less circuitous, and the words "attributable to" were used. It seems to me that the disability might be attributable to military service although it was not actually incurred during such service; I do not know whether it is or not, but that is just possible. I would suggest that we make it read "attributable to or incurred during such military service."

speakerposition: Minister of Soldiers' Civil Re-establishment; Minister presiding over the Department of Health
speechtext: I see the point. My intention was to move that we strike out in certain clauses the words " attributable to ", which appear in some other sections. The idea is to carry out what has been designated by the so'diers generally as the insurance principle. The moment disability is incurred during military service by a man who was in a theatre of war, it is equivalent to disability attributable to military service. The word " incurred " covers everything. When the disability is " incurred " during military service, it may or may not be " attributable to " service, but it is covered by the word " incurred ". It is a much more comprehensive word and the words " attributable to " are quite unnecessary, the word " incurred " covering everything.

As the section was worded last year, to the ordinary reader it would appear to have a wider interpretation than in its present form. Is there any narrowing of the application of this provision by leaving out the words " attributable to "?

speakerposition: Minister of Soldiers' Civil Re-establishment; Minister presiding over the Department of Health
speechtext: I have no objection to inserting the words " attributable to ", but they are entirely superfluous in the opinion of the pension board.

To the ordinary reader
there would appear to be very many unnecessary words and phrases in our legislation, and I do not think the minister need troub'e himself on the score of the words " attributable to" being superfluous. They might just as well be reinstated.

speakerposition: Minister of Soldiers' Civil Re-establishment; Minister presiding over the Department of Health
speechtext: Yes.

Mr. Chairman, it seems to me that if there is any possibility of the
Pension Act

interpretation of the section being narrowed the words " attributable to " should be left in. Certainly the phrase " attributable to or incurred " during military service would from the legal point of view, broaden the interpretation, and therefore the retention of the words " attributab'e to" cannot do any harm. If the section is passed in its present form', a strict interpretation might exclude a pension for any injury which did not appear until years after a man's discharge. Therefore I think if the minister has no objection'- and he says he has none-these words might well be reinstated.

Mr. Chairman, I can
see where the section might be restricted or it might be enlarged. For instance, under the old act I believe if a man suffered a disability while on leave it was not "attributable to" service; under this section it would be. On the other hand, if tuberculosis appeared one or two years after discharge, the cause of it might be very readily traced back to his military service, and in this case the omission of the words might have a restrictive effect on the interpretation of the clause. Personally I should like to see the words "attributable to" put in again, for that reason. I do not think it will work any hardship to anyone. There was a time when the clause read "attributable to his military service as such." I always objected to the last two words. They were struck out on one occasion, later they were reinstated, and then later still they were again struck out. I think those words "as such" did work mischief. To my mind the words "attributable to" should be retained for the reasons I have already stated.

It seems to me
that the omission of the words "attributable to" of necessity narrows the application of the section. A man might be gassed on service, apparently recover, and be discharged as uninjured, but later on, as the hon, member for Victoria and Carleton (Mr. Caldwell) said, tuberculosis might appear. That is a disability "attributable to" the injury "incurred" on service. The injury "incurred" on service is the gassing, it is not the tuberculosis; but the tuberculosis is the disability "attributable to" the injury, the gassing, incurred on service. So I do not think you can leave out the words "attributable to" without narrowing the application of the section.

Of course, I respect my
hon. friend's opinion. In the example he has just given the disability is due to tuber-

culosis, caused by an injury or disease which was incurred during military service.

But it was not
"incurred."

speakerposition: Minister of Soldiers' Civil Re-establishment; Minister presiding over the Department of Health
speechtext:
I should like to have just
one case indicated where the words "attributable to" would be necessary or useful. I do not think a single case can be cited. However, as I have said, I have no objection to leaving the words in. In the case cited by my hon. friend, the disability makes its appearance, let us say, two years after service. It is the disability which is pensionable, not the injury or the disease. Now, was that disability caused by an injury or disease which was "incurred" during service? It can be not "attributable to" service.
The word "caused" is not in the clause.

speakerposition: Minister of Soldiers' Civil Re-establishment; Minister presiding over the Department of Health
speechtext: Resulting from.

Have there not been
many cases of men who have been discharged as A No. 1 and who later made application for pension because their disability developed later and was attributable to service, but was not apparent on discharge? I think if we pass this clause as it stands those men would be absolutely cut out. I think the minister himself knows a number of such cases.

speakerposition: Minister of Soldiers' Civil Re-establishment; Minister presiding over the Department of Health
speechtext:
There are undoubtedly a
number of cases in which the disability made its appearance long after discharge, but this disability was found to be resulting from an injury-
"Attributable to"; and those words have been stressed repeatedly by the pension board.

speakerposition: Minister of Soldiers' Civil Re-establishment; Minister presiding over the Department of Health
speechtext:
My hon. friend, if I may
say so, does not remember exactly what has taken place. It is not the disability attributable to military service that is considered, it is the injury of disease resulting in disability. Now the disability makes its appearance, we will say, years after discharge, and is found to be the result of injury or disease which was incurred during service. This word "incurred" makes the clause a good deal wider than the words "attributable to," because the man may have incurred th_t injury or disease whilst he was absolutely outside the ranks, he might have been on leave, he might have been playing football or baseball and suffered an accident. Well, his injury would not be considered as "attributable to" military service, but it certainly would be considered as having been "incurred" during military service.

Pension Act
So I submit the word "incurred" is a good deal wider than "attributable to," and of necessity comprises the latter.

If the clause is made
to read, "was attributable to or incurred during such military service" it would have a much wider interpretation.

If this clause passes in its
present form, with the words "incurred during such military service," the scope of the act will be considerably narrowed. I have in mind the case of a man who came back from overseas and was passed as physically fit, sound in every way; but after being on his farm for a year he had to take hospital treatment, and last year he was nine months out of the twelve in hospital. He certainly is not physically fit now, but if the clause remains as it is I do not suppose there would be any possibility of his receiving consideration. I suggest that both phrases should be included.

The question is whether
the two phrases or only one should be included. Certainly the two would be stronger than the one. Since the minister indicates that it would not make any difference from his standpoint, I suggest that the words "attributable to or" be included.

In order to meet the wishes of hon. members I would move that after the -word "was" on line 16 the words "attributable to or" be inserted, so that it will read:
-when the injury or disease or aggravation thereof resulting in disability or death in respect of which the application for pension is made was attributable to or incurred during such military service.
Personally I do not see that it enlarges the provision in any way, but I am willing to have it in.
Amendment agreed to and section as amended agreed to.
On section 2-Improper conduct.

This provision was in the bill of last year. The first part of section 2 is merely a reproduction of the act as it is to-day. The only new provision is paragraph (c). It provides that in the case of any venereal disease contracted prior to service and aggravated during service in a theatre of actual war, pension shall be awarded for the whole disability, but there shall be no increase of pension afterwards.
' If the disease is contracted on service and causes death, is there any pension to the dependents?
No.

I do not see why we should make the distinction. You give pension to the man while living if he contracts this disease on service, but you do not give it to the poor unfortunates he leaves behind if he dies.

Is this clause not
identical with the clause in the bill that passed this House last year?
I think so.

From the minister's first remarks in regard to clause 1, it would seem that the pension commissioners were experiencing some qualms of conscience and were willing to widen out the provisions of the act, but now we find that on the contrary they are trying to contract. In paragraph (a) it is provided that the commission "may", when the applicant is in a dependent condition, award such pension. It seems to me the word "shall" should be used, to make it imperative. With regard to what the hon. member (Mr. Power) has just said, there is a distinction between the two classes. In one case the man has been treated and is supposed to be cured, but service brings back the trouble; in the other he incurs the disease during service.

I do not quite understand
that.
Paragraphs (a) and (b) are not new; they have been on the statute book for a number of years. As to the new paragraph (c), it is broader than the old one; it uses the word "shall"-imperative.

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext:
Section agreed to.
'On section 3-Children of pensioner classes 1-5.

This clause was in the
bill of last year. It is to extend the provision of the former act under which pensions are awarded to the children of pensioners in classes one to five when the pensioners die of a disability or disease which is not pensionable or which is not their war disability. Let me give an example:	A man who is pensioned 100 per cent on account of amputations is killed by lightning. In ordinary circumstances, in classes one to five, his dependents would not be pensionable, but in this case the dependents would be pensionable. In other words, the death is not related to service at all, but as he is a high-ddsability pensioner we make a provision in the law that his dependents shall be pensionable. That provision existed for five years in the original
Pension Act

act passed in 1919. In 1924, this House provided for an extension of that provision for five years, but that provision was defeated last year in the Senate. We are re-introducing it this year.
This section applies only to high disability pensions, 80 to 100 per cent?

speakerposition: Minister of Soldiers' Civil Re-establishment; Minister presiding over the Department of Health
speechtext: Yes.

There are many cases where women have had the care of a husband for a period of five years, the care becoming greater all the time, and if a man dies at any time after the period of five years, whether his death was due to contagious disease or any other disease not attributable to service, if his death occurred only one day after, the widow would not get a pension; but under this section she would?

speakerposition: Minister of Soldiers' Civil Re-establishment; Minister presiding over the Department of Health
speechtext: That is right.

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext:
Section agreed to.
On section 4-Pension in accord with extent of disa bility.

speakerposition: Minister of Soldiers' Civil Re-establishment; Minister presiding over the Department of Health
speechtext:
This is a new section. The first part is the same as has been provided in clause 25 of the Pension Act almost from its origin, but we make an exception for tuberculous cases. The awarding of the pension has been left an all cases to the Board of Pension Commissioners, and in exercising that discretion they have based themselves upon a certain table of disabilities, but here we are providing specifically for a certain class of pensioners, that is, the tuberculous pensioners. It will be seen that subsection (3) provides:
Pensions for disability resulting from pulmonary tuberculosis, when during the treatment of a member of the forces the presence of tubercle bacilli has been discovered in the sputum or it has been proved that the disease is moderately advanced and clinically active, sshall be awarded and continued as follows:-
Then it gives, first, the ease of the man who saw service in a theatre of actual war and who incurred tuberculosis there. He is to be pensioned for two years at 100 per cent without any possible reduction. Then there is another class of tuberculosis pensioners, those who contracted the disease during service, but who did not see service in a theatre of actual war.
Just at that point, does not subsection 3 (b) of section 4 apply only to aggravation in the case of those who did not see service in a theatre of actual war?

speakerposition: Minister of Soldiers' Civil Re-establishment; Minister presiding over the Department of Health
speechtext: No, it applies to all.

It does not say so.
Would the minister read subsection 3 (b)?
May I suggest, Mr. Chairman, though I do not like to put you to any extra work, that in view of the complicated nature of the clauses, it would make it much more simple if they were read in advance.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext:
Has each member an
underlined copy of the bill?

Yes, but one cannot read
the clause and follow the minister's explanation at the same time.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext:
I will read section 4,
taking it up subsection by subsection.

speakerposition: Minister of Soldiers' Civil Re-establishment; Minister presiding over the Department of Health
speechtext:
I think it will be sufficient, Mr. Chairman, if you start at the underlined sections, which are new.
Subsections 1 and 2 of section 4 agreed to.
On subsection 3 (a)-Pensions for pulmonary tuberculosis.
Is there any change from the present law in this section except that the pension shall be continued without reduction for a period of two years?

speakerposition: Minister of Soldiers' Civil Re-establishment; Minister presiding over the Department of Health
speechtext: There is no such provision in the act to-day.
But pensions are awarded in such cases under the law as it stands to-day.

speakerposition: Minister of Soldiers' Civil Re-establishment; Minister presiding over the Department of Health
speechtext:
No, there is no such law
to-day. This is a new clause. I may say, however, that it is the practice.
This makes it statutory.

No, I am only suggesting-

speakerposition: Minister of Soldiers' Civil Re-establishment; Minister presiding over the Department of Health

Pension Act
a period of two years without reduction. If I mistake not that was a recom-
4 p.m. mendation of a former parliamentary committee, but whether of last year or of the year before I am not certain. As I understand it, there is a provision in the old act for awarding pensions to the class of cases mentioned in this section, but the change that this section brings into effect is that the pension shall be continued now by statutory authority without reduction for a period of two years?

I have got the bearing of the subsection I referred to since the chairman has read the section. It provides that the man who saw service in a theatre of actual war shall be paid 100 per cent pension for tuberculosis if there was no aggravation, while the man who did not see service in a theatre of actual war, though he gets a pension of 100 per cent if the tuberculosis was incurred even during the other part of his service, gets only 90 per cent if there was no aggravation that might have been caused through service.

speakerposition: Minister of Soldiers' Civil Re-establishment; Minister presiding over the Department of Health
speechtext: That is right.

There are two wise provisions here which were not in the old act. One is that the pension shall continue at the full rate, 100 or 90 per cent as the case may be, for two years. The other very wise provision is that the pension shall not be reduced by more than twenty per cent at any one time, and that these reductions shall not be nearer to each other than six months, which means that the pension will not be cut off all at once, but, that the man will have a gradual chance to re-establish himself.

aggravation, just attributable to or incurred

1 think it is a
petty thing to make a provision that the disability must be increased by five per cent. I do not know how any medical man can [DOT]<ay in such cases what five per cent means. In fact, I am not altogether in favour of this provision in regard to final payment. I think if a man has a disability at any time he should be paid, even if it is two per cent, and he should not come under any provision as to final payment, because he has too much trouble getting back. He has to go to som* medical officer and get him to say that he is in a worse condition than when he was given the final payment. The man who examined him at that time perhaps cannot be found. If a man has a disability he should be paid and kept on; there has been too much cutting off. For instance, a man is asked to undergo an operation, and he has to take the operation. If he does not take it he has to get out. I do not say that those are the words, but that is the effect of it.

Just for information,
is there ever an instance where the pensioner must take final payment whether he elects to take it or not? I never was in favour of the final payment, I do not think it works well for the pensioner. I do not think he should be compelled to take the final payment.

No, but suppose
he is in this position:	That there is a suggestion whispered in his ear that if he does not take it he will have to get out and get nothing, and therefore he takes it. I do not consider it is just. I pass over the Other 	I ; i ; rij j i^i
matter, but coming down to the five per cent increase, I do not see how any person can figure it out. The five per cent should be struck out, simply leaving the word "increase." He has a hard enough time to get there at all. I have known cases where they have to chase around the country and give a doctor a fee to have the case reconsidered.

I usually find myself in general agreement with the hon. member for Kingston, and I feel he is an authority on these matters, but I must disagree in regard to the five per cent. However, I may be wrong. If this five per cent is cut out and the pension board says to a man, "Your disability is only seven or eight per cent and it does not amount to much," he may get nothing. I should like to have the view of the hon. member for Kingston on this. I think it is a safeguard to the pensioner, because, if his disability is increased five per cent, the 'board must consider his case; but if we cut out the five per cent, his disability may increase six or seven per cent, and they may not take him on.

I make this suggestion :	If we leave the word " increase "
only in the section, they would get a pension under this section. If it is two per cent, or five per cent, or ten per cent, there is no pension.

Would the minister

speakerposition: Minister of Soldiers' Civil Re-establishment; Minister presiding over the Department of Health
speechtext:
Here is the law as it stands to-day and has existed since 1919. It provides that:
No pension shall be paid to the widow of a pensioner unless she was living with him or was maintained by him or was in the opinion of the commission entitled to be maintained by him at the time of his death and for a reasonable time previously thereto.

In a case of excusable
separation or one in which a court of law would pronounce judicial separation, would the opinion of the commission be entirely in their discretion?

speakerposition: Minister of Soldiers' Civil Re-establishment; Minister presiding over the Department of Health
speechtext:
This would cover such a
case of separation, but in those cases the widow herself must not be responsible at all in the eyes of the law for having lived away from her husband.
Supposing a judicial tribunal had found in favour of the woman for a judicial separation, would the commission have the superior authority to determine otherwise?

speakerposition: Minister of Soldiers' Civil Re-establishment; Minister presiding over the Department of Health
speechtext:
I do not think they would
exercise that authority.

I have read through this
section and the amendment. This sub-clause apparently puts complete autocratic power and discretion into the hands of the commission. I am not going to take up the time of the committee in discussing difficulties and complaints that we have had in the past. This clause is going to have far-reaching effects, and I think it would be better, in the interest of the pensioners, if, in those cases where there can be no difference of opinion, for instance, the case I cited of a judicial separation, the commission should follow the findings of fact. I realize that at this stage it is difficult to make any fundamental changes, but from' my individual judgment, based on experience, I raise the objection that it is not wise to place such complete authority in the hands of the commission, by which they may make a finding contrary to the rules of judicial tribunals on questions largely of fact and law such as separation, and so on.

Is it the intention
now to reconsider cases in which a pension is being, paid but in which further payments are being withheld if in the opinion of the
Pension Act

commission the widow was indiscreet, or something of that sort?

speechtext:
Some of the subdivisions
of this subsection are quite involved and I might perhaps just briefly 'explain them. Paragraph (i) provides that if the marriage has taken place within one year after discharge, then the widow is pensionable in all cases, if the death is the result of the pensionable disability. Paragraph (ii) provides that if the marriage takes place after the coming into force of this act and the man secures from the Board of Pension Commissioners a certificate that the disability from which he suffers is not likely to result in death, then should he die from that disability the widow is .pensionable.

Can he ever get such a
certificate?

speakerposition: Minister of Soldiers' Civil Re-establishment; Minister presiding over the Department of Health
speechtext:
He might. If I had lost
a little finger and got a pension, I might go to the board and ask for a certificate that this disability was not likely to result in my death, and they would issue the certificate. But blood poisoning might develop later through an accident of some kind to that finger and I might die, and in that case my widow would be pensionable.
But that is an extremely unlikely case. Take the case of an amputated leg.

speakerposition: Minister of Soldiers' Civil Re-establishment; Minister presiding over the Department of Health
speechtext:
In that case I would not
issue a certificate.
The minister does not think that it would be possible for a man with an amputated leg to obtain a certificate that such disability might not result in death?

speakerposition: Minister of Soldiers' Civil Re-establishment; Minister presiding over the Department of Health
speechtext:
I would not give such a
certificate.

So that we may see
what value if any there is in the clause, the minister might suggest some case in which the certificate would be given.

speakerposition: Minister of Soldiers' Civil Re-establishment; Minister presiding over the Department of Health
speechtext: Paragraph (iii), I think, covers the point. It provides that in the case of a member of the forces who has married between a period of one year after his discharge and before the coming into force of this act, and who has obtained a certificate showing that any pensionable injury or disease from which he is suffering at the time of marriage would not result in death, the pension shall be allowed the widow.

The paragraph says
"who has obtained" the certificate. I take it that these words would preclude the possibility of his going to the commission after the coming into force of the act. Would it not mean that he must have secured the certificate before the passing of this legislation?

speakerposition: Minister of Soldiers' Civil Re-establishment; Minister presiding over the Department of Health
speechtext:
I do not think so; he may obtain it at any time.
Sub-paragraphs (i), (ii) and (iii) agreed to.

speakerposition: Minister of Soldiers' Civil Re-establishment; Minister presiding over the Department of Health
speechtext: Sub-paragraph (iv) relates to the man who has married between the period of one year after his discharge and the coming into force of this act and who has died of a pensionable disability. That is what we call the "prudent marriage" clause. If it may have been presumed at the time of marriage that no symptoms existed which a reasonably prudent man, making reasonable inquiries, would have known of, and if he could not have known of the existence and the potential seriousness of the injury or disease which ultimately resulted in death, then the pension shall be paid to the widow. This is going one step further.

I have in mind the concrete case of a certain Mrs. McSweyn who married a man with a pensionable disability. At the time of the marriage he had pernicious anaemia although they did not know about it. They lived on for a time and he died. Would she be entitled to a pension under the clause? They made no inquiries, for the simple reason that they suspected nothing; no prudent person is expected to inquire concerning something about which he has no suspicion at all.

Pension Act
The "prudent" clause therefore does not come into operation in this case. But would the clause cover his case, due to service?

speakerposition: Minister of Soldiers' Civil Re-establishment; Minister presiding over the Department of Health
speechtext:

prudent man made reasonable inquiries.

I put these questions because I know they are pertinent to many cases, and I thought the minister was basing the legislation on the experience and advice of the board.

On whom will the
burden of proof rest? speakerposition: Minister of Soldiers' Civil Re-establishment; Minister presiding over the Department of Health
speechtext:
Of course, if we referred
to the man's own medical documentation it is likely that the pension would be refused. My impression is that the burden of proof, if you choose to call it so, should rest on the widow or her relatives or friends.
What would be taken as proof?

speakerposition: Minister of Soldiers' Civil Re-establishment; Minister presiding over the Department of Health
speechtext: The widow would make a claim for a pension

Personally I do not
think this provision is of any value, I do not think anyone would ever get a pension under it.

speakerposition: Minister of Soldiers' Civil Re-establishment; Minister presiding over the Department of Health
speechtext: I did not draft this clause, and it is going a long distance, I must say.
Theoretically, it is.

speakerposition: Minister of Soldiers' Civil Re-establishment; Minister presiding over the Department of Health
speechtext:
Yes. could not be aware of a disability which was likely to result in death.

speakerposition: Whip of the Conservative Party (1867-1942)
speechtext:
Will the minister state the
meaning of this clause? I have read it, reread it and read it yet again, and the more often I read it the more confused I become. It seems to me with its involved language, its first proviso and its second proviso, it is impossible to reach any understandable construction of it. I presume it comes from some definite source, and no doubt the minister has a marginal note which in a few plain and distinct words will illustrate what this is intended to cover. I have really done my best, reading it over and over again, to figure out what relief it is intended to afford, but having done so I cannot reach any conclusion.

speakerposition: Minister of Soldiers' Civil Re-establishment; Minister presiding over the Department of Health
speechtext:
I am no lawyer, and if my hon. friend finds it difficult to extricate himself from the maze of this subsection, I must confess that my chances are getting slimmer and slimmer every moment. That a pension shall be paid in the case of a member of the forces who has married between the period of one year after his discharge and the coming into force of this act, and who has died of a pensionable disability prior to the coming into force of this act when the marriage took place at a time when no symptoms existed from which a reasonably prudent man, making reasonable inquiries, would have known of the existence and the potential seriousness of the injury or disease which ultimately resulted in death.

speakerposition: Minister of Soldiers' Civil Re-establishment; Minister presiding over the Department of Health
speechtext:
This is the second very
important clause of the bill. As I explained last year, the amount involved if this clause is adopted will be very large-probably $700,000 immediately, and an annual increase of about $50,000.

Will the minister explain

[Mr. Beland.l	'

speakerposition: Minister of Soldiers' Civil Re-establishment; Minister presiding over the Department of Health
speechtext: Under the act a widowed mother who is a widowed mother at the time of the soldier's death is pensionable as an ordinary widow, with a few limitations. That is, she may have an income up to $240 pei year; she may have a house of her own; she may derive, say, $2,000 from a business or occupation, but these things are not taken into account; she receives a pension as a widow of $720 a year. If she has sons or daughters who may be considered sis able to contribute to her support, there may be deducted from the pension $10 a month for each child contributing. This has been the provision of the act since 1919.

Was there not an
amendment to the act to provide that the $10 a month for each child should be deducted from the pension whether the children actually contributed to her support or not?

speakerposition: Minister of Soldiers' Civil Re-establishment; Minister presiding over the Department of Health
speechtext: Yes.

That is the law as it
now stands?

speakerposition: Minister of Soldiers' Civil Re-establishment; Minister presiding over the Department of Health
speechtext: Yes.

Was it in the law
in the first place?

speakerposition: Minister of Soldiers' Civil Re-establishment; Minister presiding over the Department of Health
speechtext: No. Now, the prospective dependent widowed mother is one who becomes a dependent widowed mother after the death of the pensioner. If the mother is a widow at the time of the pensioner's death, she comes automatically within the widowed mother's class. If after the man dies of a pensionable disability the mother becomes a dependent widow she is pensionable, under the present law, at the discretion of the board according to her need. If she has an income of $240, it is taken into account; if she earns a substantial income from her occupation, that is taken into account. And, of course, if she has sons and daughters who contribute to her support, that is also considered.
And if she earns small wages, is that not also taken into account?

speakerposition: Minister of Soldiers' Civil Re-establishment; Minister presiding over the Department of Health
speechtext:
Yes. I am referring to
the case of a widowed mother who does not come within the class of widowed mothers provided by the act. Now, if this amendment is adopted, all those mothers that are widowed to-day that are not in the widowed mother class will come automatically into that class, and the financial liability involved in the increase of their pension will be as I have stated.

Pension Act

Is it the purport of the
amendment that those coming under this class will not have their earnings or income taken into consideration when the pension is fixed?

speakerposition: Minister of Soldiers' Civil Re-establishment; Minister presiding over the Department of Health
speechtext: That is it. Private income to the extent of $240 per annum will not be considered.
But if they are not in a dependent condition they do not get any pension?

speakerposition: Minister of Soldiers' Civil Re-establishment; Minister presiding over the Department of Health
speechtext: No.

If they are earning
enough to make a living they do not get any pension; none of them do. I never could see any reason why a distinction was made between these classes of widowed mothers, and the reason there will be a large initial payment now is because those coming under this class have been held out of pension although they were not able to make a living for themselves.

speakerposition: Minister of Soldiers' Civil Re-establishment; Minister presiding over the Department of Health
speechtext:
The original idea of this
widowed mothers clause was to provide for the widowed mother whose son and only means of support went to the front and was killed. Parliament said, these widowed mothers will be considered, with a few limitations, as widows, and their income will not be taken into account in the payment of pension. Now, take the case of a soldier whose father and mother were not dependent upon him. He went to the front, came back disabled and was made a pensioner. He does not contribute toward the support of his mother or of his father; he dies of his pensionable disability; later the father dies and the widow becomes more or less dependent. She has an income of say $240, she has a house of her own, and a good position. If she is of the class of the widowed mother, she will get a pension of $720 a year under this new clause. Under the act of to-day, the board examines whether or not she is in need, and if she i3 in need they will award a pension to the maximum of 100 per cent. As a matter of fact, a number of these mothers to-day who were not widowed at the time of the man'3 death receive a full pension because they are in absolutely destitute circumstances, and in the opinion of the board had the man lived he would have contributed substantially to their support-they take that into consideration to-day and come to the help of the woman to the extent of her need. I presented this clause last year, and I want it to pass again now, or I would not have introduced it. But I want the House to know exactly
the conditions. It means that this woman will fall automatically into the widowed mother's class and that she will be pensioned as a widowed mother, with the limitations I have stated before, and this will immediately increase the pension bill by $700,000.
Is that $700,000 odd annually.

Next year it will be the

The minister in explaining this clause referred to the case of a widow having a good earning capacity,-perhaps $2,000 a year; she will receive a full pension under this section. I can quite understand the

clause was passed by the committee was to take care of cases where there was a young man going to school. speakerposition: Minister of Soldiers' Civil Re-establishment; Minister presiding over the Department of Health
speechtext:
This is a new section, never introduced in the House before. Hon. gentlemen will readily grasp the meaning of it. The clause in the act to-day reads as follows:
The pension of any female pensioner who is found to be a common prostitute, or who openly lives with any man in the relationship of man and wife without being married to him shall be suspended, discontinued or cancelled.
Some cases of hardship have been brought to my attention, one in particular from the western provinces, of which there was some mention in the House last year. This is to provide that a pension shall not be cancelled or discontinued without an opportunity being given to a pensioner to present to the commission her side of the case.
Suppose a case in which the pensioner finds that the commission has not given her a proper opportunity to explain, has she an appeal?

speakerposition: Minister of Soldiers' Civil Re-establishment; Minister presiding over the Department of Health
speechtext: No, she would not have an appeal.

In this ease we do not state how the commission is to advise the pensioner that the pension is to be cancelled. We simply say that the pensioner will obtain some kind of a hearing. Wre do not instruct the commission as to what kind of a hearing or what notice is to be given. We are not very much better off than we were before. The commission will simply say , "Yes, we wrote a letter saying we were going to cut off the pension and ten days after we cut off the pension ".

speakerposition: Minister of Soldiers' Civil Re-establishment; Minister presiding over the Department of Health
speechtext: I think the hon. member is taking an extreme view of the situation. Up to the present time a number of pensions have been cancelled in the case of widows, presumably on account of immoral conduct on the part of the pensioner, presumably without opportunity being afforded to show that the information which had been furnished to the board was erroneous.

Does the minister seriously tell me that the Board of Pension Commissioners would deliberately cancel the pension of a woman on any such grounds as those, without previously giving her a hearing? If
the board have done that in the past, they should have been fired long ago.
It has been done.

They have no business to
do it. It is a most serious thing, and they should have made it their business to make a thorough investigation into the matter.

I suggest to the minister
that the mere right of appearing before the commission is not really a protection to the persons concerned, unless they have also the right of appeal; because I have seen cases where the commission have made up their minds; you may submit a great deal of evidence, but frequently they do not show much of a disposition to change their minds. Considering the fact that it is the whole pension and is of serious consequence to the appellant, what objection would there be to allowing an appeal to the appeal board in a case of that kind?

speakerposition: Minister of Soldiers' Civil Re-establishment; Minister presiding over the Department of Health
speechtext: I think one step at a time is sufficient. This is a step in the right direction. Since the Pension Act was passed in 1919, it has been substantially amended in the years 1920, 1921J 1922, 1923, 1924 and again this year. I think we have advanced in this direction as far as we should go. The representations which have been made to me go only to the extent of providing that the widow who is to be deprived of her pension on account of immoral conduct should be offered an opportunity of presenting her case before the pension is cancelled. No claim has been made for any further amendment. I understand my hon. friend's suggestion is that an appeal should be provided in these cases, but no appeal is provided for such cases at all now. I do not say that it will not come in another session, but I suggest that we take this step this year and see how it works.
Is there any arrangement made in regard to the children of the pensioner?

It places the widow in
the same position as she was before, except that her pension will not be cut off until an appeal has been made.

speakerposition: Minister of Soldiers' Civil Re-establishment; Minister presiding over the Department of Health
speechtext:
That is correct-until her
defence is presented to the board.

I hardly think that
latter statement is correct. This act simply gives her an opportunity to present a case, but if she refuses to present any defence, her pension might be cut off. Is there any time

limit given in which she may present her
case?

speakerposition: Minister of Soldiers' Civil Re-establishment; Minister presiding over the Department of Health
speechtext: I do not think so.
I think there should be a time limit.

It is very hard to make a
time limit.

I think a number of
occurrences under the Pension Act have demonstrated to us the inadvisability of giving absolute discretion to the pension board in all these matters, and in this case there should be a time limit-six or twelve months, or whatever time the committee think necessary.
She is given an opportunity.

If we provide a time limit
the commissioners would immediately seize on that time limit, and if she came in a few minutes late she would be out of court.

The board writes her
a letter, and if she does not come back with her statement, it is left to the pension board to say that she should have come back in two or three weeks.

She can go to see a good
member of parliament, like my hon. friend from Victoria and Carleton (Mr. Caldwell).

I ask the minister
what arrangement the board had made in the ease of children of the woman who loses her pension?

speakerposition: Minister of Soldiers' Civil Re-establishment; Minister presiding over the Department of Health
speechtext: I do not think the children would be affected by it.
The children always get it.

speakerposition: Minister of Soldiers' Civil Re-establishment; Minister presiding over the Department of Health
speechtext: If the pension is paid on account of the children, the guardian will take care of the children.
Then they should come under the law of the province.

speakerposition: Minister of Soldiers' Civil Re-establishment; Minister presiding over the Department of Health
speechtext: No, there is a provision in the Pension Act for those cases.

The point I raise in
regard to the time limit I think is well taken I would like to see the amendment made effective. I think possibly we should go a step further than what has been the practice of the board. This amendment never should have been necessary. It is a very severe indictment of the practice of the pension board that it should be necessary for this parliament to pass an amendment of this kind, because under British law a person is presumed to be innocent until he is proved guilty; he should

always be given an opportunity to put up a defence. The apparent need for this amendment is the direct statement that this has not been the case in times past; I should, therefore, like to see some definite time given to these people to put in a defence.

speakerposition: Minister of Soldiers' Civil Re-establishment; Minister presiding over the Department of Health
speechtext:
In line 7 there are the
words "may direct." We might add:
And a delay of three months for such purpose shall be deemed to be reasonable.

I do not think that is long enough, as it might be difficult for a woman to assemble her evidence in three months. It would be possible for her to enter a defence in that time, if that is what is meant, and then if her case were not proven at the end of three months, I presume her pension would be cut off while her case was under consideration.

speakerposition: Whip of the Conservative Party (1867-1942)
speechtext:
I would favour a much shorter period than three months. If there were a case at all where a woman would want to be prompt in her defence, it would be one where an accusation of this kind was made against her. It stands to reason that if a notice of this kind were sent to her accusing her of such conduct and intimating that her pension was going to be cut off, two weeks or a month at the outside would be ample time for her to notify the commission that she wanted to be heard. The clause does not say that she must get in her defence within any reasonable time; it states simply that she must be given an opportunity. I remember bringing to the attention of the minister a case in my town where a woman had had her pension actually cut off without any notice, and without an interview or investigation from her standpoint. Later on when the facts were gone into, the charges which had been made against her by somebody unfriendly to her were found to be without foundation and she was reinstated. It is contrary, as my hon. friend, (Mr. Caldwell) says, to British justice that a person should be deemed to be guilty of conduct of this kind without a hearing. I understand this clause provides that before she can be deprived of her pension she must be given notice. The only thing I would suggest, if that were necessary, would be that the notice should be sent by registered letter to the address where she is receiving her pension cheques from month to month. But I think that can be left to the commission and they will no doubt send the notice there. If the woman is receiving her cheques regularly, she will get the notice. In such a case she should act promptly and one month should be ample time

Pension Act
in which to file her defence. If she is not sufficiently interested in her pension and in defending her reputation to file her defence within a month, I would never blame the pension board for cutting her off.

I would think this is
right the way it stands. I was on the committee, and the way it stands, that the pension cannot be cancelled until she 'has entered a defence, would be in her favour.

speakerposition: Whip of the Conservative Party (1867-1942)
speechtext: It says: "until an opportunity has been given."

Yes. She has to be
given an opportunity. Why limit her to a month, or any time? The cancellation cannot be made until she has had that opportunity.

Has the minister any
information as to the number of women who have had their pensions cut off without a hearing prior to the present time. Are there any such?

speakerposition: Minister of Soldiers' Civil Re-establishment; Minister presiding over the Department of Health
speechtext:
I think only two cases
were brought to my attention.

Under this provision no
such injustice will be done to a woman as to cut her pension off without a hearing?

speakerposition: Minister of Soldiers' Civil Re-establishment; Minister presiding over the Department of Health
speechtext: No.

The cases in which this clause would be brought into play must be very exceptional and the cases in which the pension board would cancel pensions would be very flagrant. With the amendment as now offered, the improvement is so great that no time limit is necessary. The amendment as it stands now might very properly be left with the pension board, and parliament at a later session may amend it if it is found to be abused.

The last provision states that any pension which has been suspended, discontinued or cancelled, may be reinstated. If there is anything in the nature of a hardship or if a widow thinks she has not had proper opportunity, that provision gives her a chance to have her pension reinstated. I think it is better without putting in any time limit at all.

There is a weakness in
the last proviso in that there is no obligation on the commission to give a reasonable opportunity for the appearance of the person concerned. They have their own authority in that connection. It is presumed, of course, that they would hear the person concerned.
It must be presumed that the pension board will act as reasonable men and carry out the spirit of the act.

Supposing a woman's
pension has been previously cancelled and she can prove that she is not guilty, it is in the discretion of the commission whether they will reinstate her pension or not. If the woman can prove her case, there should be no discretion about restoring her pension.

speakerposition: Minister of Soldiers' Civil Re-establishment; Minister presiding over the Department of Health
speechtext: It is very difficult to go to that extent. The Board of Pension Commissioners would have to examine and weigh the evidence which is brought before them and if they consider that the defence against the accusation brought against the woman is not sufficiently weighty, they may suspend the pension. The second proviso is perhaps superfluous, but I do not think it can work any injustice, nor do I think it is any reflection upon the board.

This brings up a question raised in the House last year, and I remember putting myself on record in regard to it. It should be with a great deal of hesitancy that the Board of Pension Commissioners or any board of a like nature should be placed in the position of a morality squad looking into the character of pensioners or any other group of people. Last year the case came up of a man having his pension discontinued because of boot-legging. This case was brought up by the hon. member for Kingston (Mr. Ross). Personally, I think the pension board should act very slowly about judging the character or morals of any pensioner in this country. Unless for a very flagrant breach of the ethics of life, no board should be placed in a position where a crank or a number of cranks on that board could have the right to rule out the pension of somebody or of the dependents of somebody, whose morals we did not look into when we took him overseas. I hope the minister will discourage in every possible way he can the judging of morals of pensioners unless the breach is very flagrant.

Is there no provision in the bill whereby the findings of the board in regard to the percentage of disability may be appealed from? I thought that was to be one of the provisions of the bill. The

board might find a man's disability to be 50 per cent, and as things stand now he can only put up with that. Could there not be some provision to enable him to appeal on that question?

speakerposition: Minister of Soldiers' Civil Re-establishment; Minister presiding over the Department of Health
speechtext:
Last year there was a provision for appeals on assessment but this was not passed by the Senate. At that time I had not the experience which I have since gained. The number of appeals on entitlement is so large at the present time that I do not think it would be wise to provide for any appeal on assessment. The number of appeals would naturally be very large; any man would be open to appeal his appraisal of disability. It would cost him nothing; it would be only a matter of a move on the part of the pensioner to have his assessment made 40 per cent instead of 30, or 30 instead of 20, or 70 instead of 50 as the case might be. I have consulted the members of the Board of Appeal on this point and have asked their opinion regarding the desirability of appeals on assessment, and they have sent me a memorandum in this connection which has confirmed me in the opinion that it would not be wise at present to provide for such appeals. We have 44,000 disability pensioners every one of whom, except those who are 100 per cent disabled, would be eligible for appeal if they chose to take advantage of such a provision. Of necessity therefore the number of appeals would run into tens of thousands. Moreover, the fixing of disability on re-examination would' be subject to appeal as well. So that my hon. friend will realize that the Board of Appeal would be so overwhelmed that it would be well nigh impossible for them to consider appeals on assessment for a year and a half or at least a year. The number of entitlement appeals now entered is 4,738; of these, 1,567 have been ruled upon as being not within the board's jurisdiction; 1,060 have been heard, and 2,111 remain still to be dealt with. During the period of January 1, 1925, to March 31, 1925, 1,005 individuals filed appeals with the board. The board works assiduously, hearing, on an average 102 cases per month, which I think is rather large in view of the fact that it must hear the representative of the soldier and examine into his documents which generally are voluminous. The board have to weigh all the evidence before they reach a decision. So, at the rate of 102 cases per month it would take them at least one year and ten months to dispose of all those entitlement cases. I am afraid it would clog the wheels of the appeal board.

Pension Act
if we were to allow appeals on assessment. I think the time will come when we will have to allow such appeals, or at least appeals from final awards. We do not have final awards as yet, but I think we should have them. They have them in England and in the United States. These final awards cover what it is a decided pensioner should be paid during the rest of his life whether his disability remains stationary or not. We have what are known as permanent cases, but there is no finality about them, because should the disability increase the amount of pension may be increased after one, two or three years; and should the disability decrease the amount of pension may be reduced. I think it should be in order before very long to provide for final awards. There would be some abjection taken by the returned men, but generally speaking the great majority of them would agree that the final award system should be adapted in Canada. If we allowed appeals on assessment, as I explained to the delegation which met me on this subject, we may have as many as 50,000 appeals during one year, and it is the opinion of the board that the provision might lead to frivolous appeals. Of course we would admit that entitlement appeals should be heard first. I am advised that we may expect appeals at the rate of from 50 to 75 per month for an indefinite period. So I cannot see just now that it would be possible to effectively deal with appeals on assessments.

Would it not be
possible-I think the minister admits that it will be necessary in the future, if not now- to set up a separate tribunal to try appeals on assessment? When he says that every pensioner, except 100 per cent disability cases, would have the right to appeal, I think he has forgotten section 15 of the act that passed this House last session. It placed certain restrictions on the right to appeal on assessment, and is as follows:
15. Subsection one of section eleven of chapter sixty-two of the statutes of 1923, is repealed and the following is substituted therefor:
(1) Upon the evidence and record upon which the Board of Pension Commissioners gave their decision an appeal shall lie in respect of any decision of the said Board of Pension Commissioners, provided that in cases of assessment appeals the appellant shall be required (a) to obtain the consent of an official soldiers' adviser before presenting his appeal; (b) to present certificates of examination from two independent qualified medical practitioners in the form of statutory declarations on approved forms which shall contain an estimate of the percentage of disability, and (c) that the estimated percentage of disability as set out in the certificates provided for shall indicate the appellant's condition to be at least two classes higher than he has been assessed by the Board of Pension Commissioners.
182i
This was threshed out very thoroughly by the committee fast session, and we thought that by inserting this restriction we would, to use a common expression, "put them over the sieve"-the trivial ones would be sorted out, and only the deserving cases would come to the attention of the appeal board. There is one other point in connection with the request or an appeal on assessment. It is a point I supported very strongly last session, and I still support it-that if the pension board admit attributability under the present act, and only give a 5 per cent pension, the man is out of court, although he might be entitled to 40 per cent or even more. There have been probably more hardships in respect to this matter than there have been in respect to the absolute cutting off of pensions. The minister would do well to consider it seriously before he shuts the door. He has always been inclined to do justice to returned men in the matter of pension, but I cannot help thinking there should be a right of appeal here, even if it is necessary to set up a separate tribunal to hear appeals on matters of assessment.

A man at some point
distant from Ottawa may be found upon medical examination to be entitled to a certain disability, but when the return is made to the central office at Ottawa the decision of the local medical authorities is overruled or a decreased pension is awarded, with resulting injustice to the pensioner. It seems to me that in these cases the pensioner should have the right to appeal to a higher tribunal; he should not be entirely subject to the arbitrary and dictatorial authority of the officials in Ottawa who do not know his case, who have not the knowledge and information they should have to enable them to make a wise decision. The minister would be well advised to consider the right of that class of case to an appeal to the Eederal Appeal Board.

I do not know at what other point I could very well introduce them. I wanted to ask the minister's opinion upon this question: A soldier, a transient passing through a municipality, becomes ill and is taken off the train. Toronto Harbour Commissioners
