The House resumed at eight o'clock. TORONTO HARBOUR COMMISSIONERS
The House in committee on Bill No. 42, to amend the Toronto Harbour Commissioners Act, 1911.-Mr. Church-Mr. Gordon in the chair.

I think the hon. member
in charge of the bill should explain what it is about.

The object of this bill is to amend the original powers of the commission ratified by this parliament in 1911 by adding thereto these three sections. At Sunnyside, in the western part of the city between the Humber river to Sunnyside there has been erected on filled in lands a park and playground for the people of the city of Toronto, solely at the expense of the city. No government money has been spent on this project or playground. The amount involved is a little over three million dollars for the boulevard, driveway reclamation and buildings.
There are two parties to this bill; one is the city council, which supplied the money to the harbour commission on the bonds of the harbour commission, guaranteed by the city; so that it is all civic money involved. The government built a breakwater there and made the expenditure for it themselves. I may say that when the act was passed previous ' to this the people voted on this whole harbour proposition and approved of it. Fifty per cent of the money was expended for the park and boulevard scheme by the harbour commission and fifty per cent by the city. There are twelve miles of waterfront, and the commission bought out and obtained control of this whole waterfront, to be used for the benefit of the public forever. Half of the whole scheme was industrial and half park.
The sole object of the bill is to validate the expenditures of one unit at Sunnyside. The cost of the park and recreation grounds has been paid by the city. The people as I said, voted on the project and approved of it. This bill was presented to the city council and passed unanimously by that body. The Private Bills committee went into the whole matter 'and passed the bill unanimously.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
According to the law
the harbour commissioners are under the supervision and control of the Department of

Toronto Harbour Commissioners
Marine and Fisheries. Has this bill been submitted to the Department of Marine and Fisheries, and has it been approved of?

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: The hon. member knows bills are never submitted to the departments. They would be referred at the request, I presume, of the minister of the appropriate department to the appropriate committee. I think that has been done in this case.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
My right hon. friend
knows all bills concerning harbour commissions are public bills introduced by the Minister of Marine and Fisheries, and I see by the annotation that this is an amendment to chapter 26 of the statutes of 1911, which is a public statute. This is a private bill purporting to amend a public bill. I do not say that there is anything wrong about it, but I think it should at least have been submitted to the department under which all harbour commissions come.

Might I explain, for the
benefit of the minister, that the Department of Marine and Fisheries are consulted only where their work actually is and that is out on the harbour proper, or as affecting navigation. This work is on the shore and it has always belonged to the city. It is all on unimproved land owned by the city. We have filled it in and carried out a nice park scheme. The minister, I think, has been there and has seen the work. The harbour commission was reconstituted in 1911 when the government made an arrangement whereby three commissioners are appointed by the city council and two by the government. The city spends its own money through this harbour board. The Dominion government spends its money outside of the harbour on the local water through the Public Works department. This particular bill is just a validation of what has been done at Sunnyside by the city on its own lands through the harbour commission. The Department of Marine and Fisheries are consulted, and in every case they have given their approval of every bit of the work done in their own field, which is out on the actual waterfront. This is purely a park scheme at Sunnyside west of the exhibition grounds. The land and the money spent all belong to the city. The whole harbour programme was submitted to the various government departments and the whole scheme has been approved from time to time. They are heartily in favour of it. Sunnyside is a great picnic ground and park centre for the people of Toronto. The reason we come here is to vali-

date to 'let the government know that we are partners with them in this scheme. Although this has not cost the government a single cent, we are here to let the government know what we are and have been doing ourselves on the city end of it.

I would suggest that the
hon. member allow the bill to stand until the Minister of Marine and Fisheries (Mr. Cardin) is in his place. It seems unreasonable that this bill should be pressed forward tonight. It appears to be a matter pertaining to the harbour commission of Toronto and the minister is not present. This comes under the Harbour Commissioners Act. If the bill is all right, there is no doubt the minister would approve it. If it is not all right, it should not be rushed through without notice. _

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: The minister must know what the system is. There is someone in the department whose business it is to watch any legislation, private or otherwise, affecting that department. This applies everywhere. Certainly, the minister, having learned of this bill, would have taken steps to have had objection. taken to it before the committee if the department had any objection. It is hardly fair to ask the hon. member to postpone his bill because the minister is not here. It is not his fault that the minister is not here. On its face, the bill does not appear to be one in which the Department of Marine and Fisheries would be concerned, for the reason that it affects such portion of the harbour commission's work as is carried on wholly out of Toronto money and not out of public money at all.

Is the public money and
Toronto money not put into the same fund?

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: No.

I am familiar
with this undertaking. This particular phase of the work is something which was entered upon as a civic improvement. Some people in Toronto think-and they are in the majority at the present time-it is better that it should be handled through a commission instead of through the city council, and the city council spends its money in connection with this Sunnyside improvement through the harbour board, the council having confidence in the harbour board. The reason why this bill is brought into this House is very simple. The commissioners have gone ahead as they have, thinking they had every legal right to do it, acting, as they were, as trustees for the city and spending municipal money, and

Toronto Harbour Commissioners
have done the work. The works are there. The amusements go on, the harbour board collecting the revenues and rentals. The question was raised whether they had any legal right to do this. What we are doing here is merely legalizing what is already done, and we are doing it, as hon. gentlemen will see, in connection with a matter which has absolutely nothing to do with Dominion activities. The harbour board are chosen, not because they are the harbour board, but because they are a body of men in whom the municipality has confidence, and their actions in running this park have absolutely nothing to do with their jurisdiction as a harbour board. But as they are the creation of the Dominion, if there be any question as to their legal powers, this is the proper place to come.

speakerposition: Minister of Labour
speechtext:
My hon. friend might
have noticed in a very prominent paper the other day great criticism of the government for the money which had been and is now being expended in assisting to create and maintain an amusement park at Sunnyside for the people of Toronto. My hon. friend may be entirely right in saying that no federal money is being spent on this project, but my judgment has always been that this is a part of the general harbour improvement scheme of the city of Toronto and that a fair proportion of federal money has been expended from the Humber down to the old fort.
What paper was that? I should like to have a look at it.

speakerposition: Minister of Labour
speechtext:
My recollection is that
it was the Montreal Gazette, or the Standard.

That would be
the Standard.

speakerposition: Minister of Labour
speechtext: It is a constant criticism. I am not complaining, but my understanding is-and I think if my hon. friend inquires a little more closely, he will find I am right- that some public money has been spent there in filling up the property.

The federal aid has not been sufficient to look after the harbour itself. The city has spent, prior to the present time, more money than the government has, and city moneys are going into the harbour proper which ought to be entirely a government expense. As regards government money, the government contract is not even implemented. As a result of concessions of land and the undertaking of responsibility by the municipalities, there is the government's straight contract that a bridge is to be built to the island, making that island useful. This has not been done. Instead of the government having spent more money in Toronto than Toronto is entitled to for harbour improvements, the fact is that the government has not implemented its promises. The contract still stands, and the fact is that, instead of spending too little money, if anything Toronto has spent far too much.

speakerposition: Minister of Labour
speechtext:
Is it not a fact that
there is just one Toronto harbour improvement scheme running from the Humber to Scarborough and including the entire shore line of Toronto, and that the works at Sunnyside are a part of that improvement scheme?

If my hon.
friend thinks that a merry-go-round is part of a harbour improvement, he is quite right; but nobody except my hon. friend would ever think that a merry-go-round, switch-backs and bathing houses are part of a harbour improvement. This is something which is super-added entirely by the municipality at its own expense. The only reason it is connected with the harbour matter is, as I have already explained, that the harbour board is a body of men doing work in the vicinity whom the city council think, are better able to look after this work than the city itself.

Since confederation the
government has assumed responsibility for the shore protection of the harbour at Toronto, and off Sunnyside erected a breakwater. The city paid the entire cost of the park and filling. The government has spent, since 1867, only 86,000,COO or $7,000,000 on Toronto harbour and the revenue from concessions in this park annually is between $90,000 and $100,000.
Some legal advisers were of opinion that it was not necessary to come to parliament for an amendment such as is here proposed to the Harbour Act of 1911; they thought that there was power enough in the act to enable the commissioners to go on with the work. But some doubt was raised a short time ago and it was thought better to apply for an amendment to clear up any doubt in the matter. The words in the statute of 1911 enabled the commissioners to " hold, develop, maintain and improve " the place and it was thought that in these four words they had the power to go ahead. This bill is simply declaratory; the object is to make the act perfectly clear. The breakwater at Sunnyside was constructed by the government itself, but there was nothing behind the breakwater at all; and so far as the actual amusement park is concerned the newspaper quoted is entirely in error; the government has not contributed a cent to its creation and upkeep.

Sunnyside beach is situated at the extreme west end of the city and extends along the lake shore from the Humber river on the west to Wilson avenue on the east, a distance of one and a half miles. It contains about 120 acres of land all of which has been reclaimed. Through this area runs a boulevard drive fifty feet wide and a lake shore promenade twenty-four feet wide. The bathing pavilion is a concrete structure four hundred feet by one hundred and twelve feet and has accommodation for 7,700 bathers at one time. The amusement resort contains restaurants and refreshment booths, band stands, dodgem, frolic, whip, old mill, Sunny-side racer, aero swing, merry-go-round, shooting gallery, games, guess weighing machines, putting green and baseball diamond. All concessions are under the control of the harbour commissioners, they are leased to concessionaires at a nominal rental plus a percentage of the gross receipts. With the exception of the bathing pavilion, all the concessions are operated by the lessees who have already expended upwards of $500,000 on amusement devices and buildings. Nearly four millions have been spent on park and driveway, filling and boulevard.
Altogether, this is one of the finest amusement parks to be found in any city of the same size on the continent. The people voted on the whole harbour bill, and as I have already said this amendment to the 1911 act is only declaratory legislation; it is merely intended to clear up the intention of the statute of 1911. I hope that there will be no difficulty about passing the bill. The lands were filled in before the breakwater was constructed as a whole. The commissioners get no salary. They were working to get control of the waterfront for the public.
Who paid for the ground which is now used for amusements. Was it paid for with the money of the federal government?
It was the city's money. The government paid for the breakwater.
Well, do I understand that the breakwater was paid for with federal money?
Yes.

I understand further that
the merry-go-round and the other amusements situated behind the breakwater could not have been put up unless the breakwater had previously been built. If I am not right in that statement I wish to be corrected. Am I wrong?
IMr. Church.]

Yes. As this is in my
riding perhaps I might foe permitted to say a word about it. The government and the city collectively constructed the breakwater and the city did the filling in behind. That is how the thing started. The city then went on filling in and improving the land and they spent a lot of money; the government did not spend any money at all on this. The money was taken out of the pockets of the taxpayers of the city-money that was wasted. Why. even the tops of a farm were brought down to make a top dressing for a Parkdale boulevard and bathing ground, and when they got it finished it was inhabited principally by Jews. The Jews occupied it and even put a sign up, something to this effect, "After the war we gave you Palestine; for Heaven's sake let us have Sunmyside." The city found itself in possession of a large acreage of ground but it had not the power either to lease or to sell it or to establish any permanent improvement. All that this bill contemplates and all it asks is to validate the city in the power to lease this property made by the filling in of the land behind the breakwater, and to establish thereon amusements suitable to a sumlmer resort; and to loan money to any corporation or company that might operate there. That is all there is to it. Not a dollar of government money has gone into the park to which this bill relates. We simiply ask that the old act .foe so amended that the city shall have that power; otherwise the place will remain a grass plot. They cannot get anyone to occupy it because they cannot give a lease long enough to make it worth while for people to construct any merry-go-rounds or amusement buildings that are required to make the thing a going concern. There is no harm whatever in the bill; there is no liability on the part of the government, although there is a considerable liability on the part of the local taxpayers. I ask that the bill be passed. The council have agreed on the matter; and although the original bill which my hon. friend brought down was a very serious one they have modified it now, having come to a satisfactory decision among themselves. I think they have produced a bill which is absolutely innocent and as reasonable as we could hope the present council of the city of Toronto could draw up having regard to the taxpayers. Hon. gentlemen need have no hesitation about passing the bill; and the trepidation of my hon. friend (Mr. Power) is, I was going to say, altogether sectional.

Toronto Harbour Commissioners

I think I am entitled to receive the congratulations of the House on having drawn out my hon. friend (Mr. Sheard) who has made an able, lucid explanation of the manner in which the Toronto city council had arranged to settle any disputes that might have arisen over those which took place at Geneva in the League of Nations. The Toronto city council has, I think, dealt with a question which has been disturbing, one might almost say, the peace of nations for several centuries; and it has dealt with that question well: It has placed the Jews in one of the best parts of Toronto. But I do not think that this answers all the objections which I was about to raise, one of which was that this amusement park could not have been constructed had not the federal government first furnished the funds for a breakwater behind which the city filled in and laid out playgrounds. As to the other objection, I may be mistaken in this portion of my remarks when I say that I understand that the harbour commissioners of Toronto receive a certain remuneration for their services.
No.

Do they give their services
gratuitously?
They all do, but I do not know whether the chairman gets anything or not. But he is here; you can ask him.

To judge from the work
which that hon. gentleman does on behalf of the city of Toronto and Toronto harbour in this House I should think he ought to be handsomely paid. Of course if the commissioners are not paid, my remarks have no bearing on the subject. I was about to object to the harbour commissioners, paid by the federal government, devoting any of their time to collecting money for amusements. But I think my original objection still remains, that the federal government have indirectly, and possibly very directly, contributed largely to a work which, after all, is not in the public interest of the Dominion, that is to say, the placing of a bathing beach for the use of certain well-known and highly respected citizens of Canada residing in the city of Toronto. One of the principal characteristics of those citizens is that they certainly are able to look after themselves financially-usually they take everything in a financial way that is not nailed down, and I do not know just why the other citizens of Canada should be called upon to contribute to their enjoyment.

Mr. Chairman, in answer
to the hon. member for Quebec South (Mr Power), let me say that the whole shore line where this particular breakwater is built was being washed away every season. This work was constructed, in part, by the Dominion government, the estimates being passed in this House in the way that we would vote estimates for work in any other part of the Dominion where the federal government is responsible. Inasmuch as the breakwater was built to protect not only the shore line but also the main line of the old Grand Trunk -now the Canadian National-and the vacant -space was there to be filled in, why not put it to some use so that revenue could be derived from it? I do not for one moment think that it is to the credit of the hon. gentleman to cast reflections on honourable men, whether harbour commissioners in the city of Quebec or in the city of Toronto, who many times during each week, year in and year out, give of their services for the benefit of their native towns. If my hon. friend will just glance back over the last ten or twelve years since these harbour commissioners have been giving their services freely for the benefit of their communities-

May I ask what reflection
I cast on any harbour commissioners?

If he will bear in mind
those harbour commissioners, I think he will agree with me that they are gentlemen of the very highest calibre not only in the city of Quebec but also in the city of Toronto.
Mr. Chairman, may I ask-

Let me say, Mr. Chairman, that at the present time in the city of Toronto the gentlemen of Liberal leanings who are on the harbour commission of that city are, in my opinion, deserving of a great deal of credit not only from the citizens of Toronto but also from the members of the Liberal party who occupy the treasury benches.

speechtext:
Having the honour of representing the constituency through which the proposed railway will run, if it happens to pass the Senate this year, and knowing the country as intimately as I do, I have no hesitation whatever in saying that that road should be built. I have lived in that part of the
C.N.R.-Branch Lines

country now for over eighteen years and I know the inhabitants and settlers intimately. They opened up that country between forty and fifty miles from the city of North Battle-ford away back in 1905, and they were promised when they went into the Rabbit lake country, that if they would only go in there and open up the country, within a year or two they would have railway communication. That country was opened up with a first-class type of settler, Englishmen, Scotchmen, Irishmen, Canadians and Americans very largely. Time after time their hopes of railway communication have been dashed to the ground. Somehow or other the official promises that were given were not kept, and a few of the settlers started to leave the country after building up a decent home to live in. They found out that it was utterly impossible for them, under conditions before the war, to raise farm produce and market it when they had to haul it a distance of anywhere from forty-five to sixty miles. Last winter when I was in the city of North Battle-ford I saw one man coming in with two loads of wheat from a distance of over sixty-five miles. The wheat was grown in a country the crops of which were better than seventy-five per cent of the crops in northern Saskatchewan. In the year 1912-13, I think it was, the provincial government were so convinced that this was a necessary road that they guaranteed the bonds for some forty miles, and the proceeds of those bonds are applicable to a part of the line provided for in the bill at the present time.
When the war broke out the settlers in that country did not for one moment keep agitating for the railway. Instead of that practically every young man in that country enlisted, went overseas and fought at the front, and many a schoolhouse in that district to-day has a little brass tablet on the wall placed there in memory of the boys who went to the front and gave all for their country. After the war the question of railway construction again became a paramount one. The Canadian Northern Railway had promised to build into that district, and as I said a moment ago, their bonds had been guaranteed. In the year 1920 the Canadian Pacific Railway applied for a charter to build a road from Cory, near Saskatoon, to Birch lake, practically paralleling the proposed Canadian Northern road the whole way. A strong deputation of gentlemen from that district came down here prepared to support the application of the Canadian Pacific Railway, but the hon. gentleman who represented that constituency at that time, acting I be-
lieve under pressure of the government of that day, fought very strenuously against the Canadian Pacific Railway getting the charter. The Hon. Dr. Reid, who was Minister of Railways at that time, told that deputation personally that if the Canadian Pacific Railway did not get their charter the Canadian National Railways would immediately start in to build that road from Turtleford to Hafford, upon the branch line running from North Battleford to Prince Albert. The deputation, after putting up a strenuous fight, went away satisfied that Dr. Reid would carry out his promise and I understand that he did. Contracts were let for, I think, forty miles, but only twenty-three miles of the grade were completed. The reason I understand that more was not done was that labour at that time was very difficult to get, wages were very high and, as the contractor has told me several times, it was a practical impossibility for him to get enough labour to fulfil the whole of his contract. In another chamber la^t year an hon. gentleman, in seconding the resolution that this bill should be laid over for another year practically said that this work had been given in that country to help out the settlers because they had no work to do. Probably that hon. gentleman was misinformed by someone or another because the contractor told me an entirely different story. During the second session after this government came into power, they brought in a bill covering a number of branch lines and we know the fate that befell that bill. Last year this was brought in as a separate bill and to the astonishment, I think, of hon. members, this bill was again defeated. During the various stages which this bill took both in this House and in the railway committee last year, not one objection or argument was put forward against it.	I hope this year it will receive the
support of every hon. member in this House and that the Senate will see its way clear to let the bill for this railway go through.
I should like to say a word or two about the country because I know it intimately. The country through which this railway goes is one of the best districts in northwestern Saskatchewan. The twenty-three miles that have already been graded have been graded through the very roughest part of the whole line. We hear a good deal about mixed farming at the present time and this is an ideal district for mixed farming. There is something in that district which is unique in western Canada. Let me give this illustration to show hon. members the type of men and women who are farming there. A man

C.N.R.-Branch Lines
has gone in there and established a creamery which is fifty miles away from a railway depot. He is making good, and last year at this point, fifty miles away from a railway, he turned out over 100,009 pounds of butter. That shows the type of country this is and the type of men who are settling there. These men and women are well nigh hopeless of getting railway accommodation, and I get letters from them day after day. Last year after the session was over I travelled all through that country, and to the very best of my ability I pleaded with those men and women to stay and try it out for one more year because I believed this year the railway would come to a successful fruition. They *have spent in that district over $150,000 on roads, and the roads are good. You can go all through that district with a car and you will not be stuck in mud holes or anything else. The whole district has been organized into school districts. In some parts of it we have a foreign population, and these boys and girls are being brought up and educated to the true ideals of British citizenship. I would plead with hon. members of this House and, from my place here, with hon. members of the Senate at least to give this railway to these men and women who have had the grit and determination to stay in that district. The type of country is such that neither this government nor the provincial government has yet had to give a dollar's worth of relief to those settlers. We do not owe any money in that district for seed grain and relief. Relief has been granted in exceptional cases, but the local municipalities themselves have always successfully financed their own affairs. They have granted their own relief and they have paid for seed grain for their settlers. Once more, I do hope that this bill will have a successful passage through this House and through the Senate. If any people in this country have earned and deserve the right to railway communication, the people in that district certainly have.
Sir HENRY DRA.YTON: The last time the bill for this line went through this House, it went through without any discussion at all. It was taken as read. There was no objection except that it ought to be in the estimates. It is a good thing that we should have a little discussion on it now, so that it cannot be said that the House was entirely asleep when it passed this legislation. I have been greatly impressed by what my hon. friend (Mr. Davies) has said. The great thing we want in connection with these branch line bills is to have the lines built where they are really needed, not in places where there
are other lines, nor where they are not a crying necessity. As a matter of fact, it is a crime to build a railway where it is not absolutely a crying necessity. My view is that where you have agricultural land as you have it in the west, there comes a point beyond which no one should be asked to haul grain or produce or anything else. This is not any new view. I have always held it. The hon. member has shown-and my recollection bears him out and it is by reason of that recollection that I did not oppose this bill last year-that farmers there are hauling their produce, I think he said, sixty-two miles. I have always felt that any haul in the west involving more than a day is a haul which cannot be looked upon as practical or economic, and I still maintain that view. Here we have a place where the haul is very heavy. Hon. gentlemen to my left say that a ten-mile haul is sufficient. No, we can do with longer hauls than that in the west and the west does not mind that. The people of the west are willing to take their produce greater distances as long as they can do the one thing which is necessary, and that is, make farming pay. To do that they must be able to look after that haul in a day. That I look upon as an absolute minimum of railway accommodation which we should try to give them. These oases of real necessity ought to be looked after, and if we look after too much, we are in peril of not properly looking after them. We should be very sure in connection with every railway project, first, that the line is not a political line, second, that it is a proper construction in the public interest. I see no reason why this bill should not pass.

speakerposition: Minister of Railways and Canals
speechtext:
The Canadian National
board made a certain agreement with the city of Regina in regard to some outstanding differences, agreeing to give their reasonable support to the city in the construction of this line. Among other things, a hotel was projected by the Grand Trunk Pacific Railway some years ago in the city of Regina and that hotel was partly constructed. The Canadian National did not wish to go on with the completion of it and, reasonably I might say, the government did not wish to encourage them to carry it out. Certain streets had been closed by the city for the railway, and certain properties had been given; arrangements had been made for the construction of a station, and all that sort of thing. In order to abrogate the whole agreement that had been made between the city and the Grand Trunk Pacific, this new agreement was arrived at as a sort of clearing house of all differences, and the Canadian National recommended this bill in pursuance of their promise to give reasonable support to the wishes of the city for the construction of the line.

The minister is no doubt
aware that one of the best hotels in Regina was sold under the hammer since this recommendation was made to him.

speakerposition: Minister of Railways and Canals
speechtext: That is all the more reason why we should not build the hotel.

This is a most extraordinary proposal. The only justification for this line of railway seems to be the fact that a certain railway company in the past defaulted in the construction of a hotel. I think thait probably the minister knows of some other reason for building this road and I should like to hear it.

speakerposition: Minister of Railways and Canals
speechtext:
Now I will give the additional reason; I felt sure that what I said a moment ago was what hon. gentlemen wanted to know first. The statement I made first was in reply to the question as to who was the promoter of the line. The following memorandum explains the question-the clause an regard to the hotel I will not read, having already explained it:
It is proposed in 1925 to call for tenders for grading if possible, to be completed during that year, at an estimated cost of approximately $397 000, including right of way, and so on. In 1926, it is intended to lay the track, ballast the line and generally complete it at an estimated cost of $544,000 for the year.

C.N.R.-Branch Lines
The line will run from Avonlea to a point on the Regina-Boundary branch, about five miles south of Regina.
The object of the line is to give a direct connection into Regina from the Gravelbourg branch, and also from the territory in the vicinity of Radville. It will also make saving to the railway in hauling grain off the Gravelbourg branch. In fulfilment of an agreement reached with the city of Regina, authority to construct this line is being sought in lieu of cancellation of an obligation contracted by the Grand Trunk Pacific Railway to construct and operate a hotel in the city of Regina.
The saving to the railway for short routing the grain is estimated at $27,000 per year. Not less than $1,500,000 would have been required to finish the proposed hotel in Regina which would have imposed a fixed charge of $75 ,000 per year; besides it is considered the hotel would have made an operating loss of some $50,000 per year. Against these savings of $152,000 are the fixed charges of the cost of the line of $47,050, the fixed maintenance of way of $29^700, and the annual cost of an interlocker with the Canadian Pacific Railway estimated at $5,000, or, a total of $81,750 per year, showing a net saving of about $70,250 per annum.
There would be something like 80,000 acres of territory, all of good farming land given closer railway connection, thus offering some assistance to farmers on the route.
Has the minister looked over the map carefully to see where the road is running, so that he may give us his own judgment on this branch line?

Mr. Chairman, I am not personally interested in this district at all, but recently I received through the mail a map of it, and I may say that I am heartily in agreement with the principle laid down by the hon. member for West York (Sir Henry Drayton) as one that should govern the building of these lines-that the first consideration should be the placing of farmers within a reasonable distance of their market. As I looked over that map I was forced to the conclusion that there is absolutely no justification for the building of the line when there are so many other places that are very much removed from railway facilities. I know the minister (Mr. Graham) is not giving us reasons that seriously -weigh in his own mind why this line should be constructed, and I am confident its construction will not appeal to the members of this House.

Mr. Chairman, it so happens that this line passes through the district that I have the honour to represent, so it may not be out of place for me to say a word or two in regard to it. I should like to discuss the railroad situation for one minute if the committee will bear with me. A system of centralization has grown up in Canada. Everything that it is possible to centralize in Montreal, is centralized there; if it slips by Montreal it is stopped at Toronto; if it slips by Toronto it goes to Winnipeg. But I
want to say to hon. gentlemen that that great territory between Winnipeg and the Rocky mountains, a thousand miles long and as wide as you like, is represented by men in this corner of the House who do not believe in centralization. We believe in decentralization. Transportation is our great problem in that country, and we want the long hauls for the carload lots and the short hauls for the expensive local freights.
Let me show you what they have done to us in years gone 'by. Fifteen years ago the Canadian Pacific Railway started a railroad from Weyburn to Lethbridge, a distance of 445 miles. They built the line within 25 miles of Lethbridge-no mean city and, the natural distributing point of that country-and then they said, "We have not got any money to go further." About the same time they started a line from Moose Jaw southward' that would strike the Lethbridge line at Assiniboia 111 miles west of Weyburn, but when they got within 15 miles they said, "We have got no more money we cannot complete it." The consequence was that for years we had to bring our coal, our lumber and our fruit 800 miles further than would have been necessary had that little gap been built. I say to members of this House, we do not like that kind of thing. A few years ago they started a line from Avonlea to Swift Current-another city of no mean pretensions. They got 122 miles built, and the members of this House have been fighting year after year to get that line extended to Swift Current, but always the answer is, "We have no money." For lack of that line being completed we have to switch all our lumber, all our fruit, all our cement and the hundred and one other things we need around by Avonlea, 150 miles further than would be necessary if they had put in that little kink. And now they ask for a line to go across to Regina, a million dollar line running right through my district, and a number of my constituents send me letters and telegrams saying, "Mr. Hopkins, support the line. We gave you a good vote last time." I will tell those people that we have got too many lines in too many places, and I will also tell them that they have been built because of just such letters being sent as those sent to me. I will tell them that I consider it a crime for me to support that line when there are people in that country drawing their grain for forty and fifty miles. I will tell them that if they put that line across that territory to Regina, that will be another million-dollar white elephant. We have put on six hundred of them in the last five years, and Canada cannot stand any

C.NJt.-Branch Lines

more. Now, I know that that is not going to get me any votes, but I am going to tell you that it is not necessary that I get votes, it is not necessary that I come back to this House, but it is necessary that some men in this country stand up like men and denounce such projects.

Mr. Chairman, this
proposed line runs across one corner of the constituency which I represent, and I think perhaps I had better say a few words too, for fear I do not get all the votes I should. Now, the minister has not explained to us what, legal claim the city of Regina holds against the government to carry out the agreement of the Grand Trunk Pacific with the city. I think the government should show us that we are really legally obligated to the city in this matter. It is claimed that the Grand Trunk Pacific had agreed to build in the city a hotel. Now, the story of how that proposition was put on is, I think, very illuminating. A bunch of real estate men, back in the good old palmy days of 1910, 1911 and 1912, got together and secured an option on a lot of property around where the proposed hotel was to be built. Then they got busy in an effort to have the city of Regina bonus the Gland Trunk Pacific. Some other citizens in Regina who were not in on this scoop also got busy and showed that it was against the law of the province for a municipality to bonus any such project, and! they engaged a lawyer to institute proceedings for an injunction. But there were so many influential citizens in on this real estate scoop that they brought pressure to bear on the lawyer to drop the case, and before a legal man could be got from Moose Jaw or Winnipeg to take it up, the legislature passed a special act enabling the city of Regina to bonus the Grand Trunk Pacific. Then these enterprising people got busy, dug a hole up on Albert street and stuck up a framework of steel a mile away from where it should !be. That is as far as they proceeded with their hotel. Now.it is just such manipulation and unbusinesslike procedure as that which wrecked the Grand Trunk Pacific and some of our other railways, and if the government is going to proceed along the same course we shall be pulled down too. We have got to come to a stopping place.
_ There is no real necessity for this hotel, it has been abandoned, but to satisfy some citizens in Regina it is now proposed to build a line from Regina across to Avonlea. There is not a farmer in that district that has to go over twelve miles at the outside to a Station, and ten miles catches very nearly all 
of them. The country is all under cultivation, it is well served by railroads to-day, and there is no more necessity for this branch line than there is for the hotel, not a bit. It will take a let of trade away from Moose Jaw city and land it in Regina, but that would be no benefit to the district. That is not what we are here to look after. The Canadian National Railways have enough burdens to bear without our loading them up with another million-dollar liability. The minister said this line would give sendee to Radville. I received a letter from the Radville Board of Trade to-day asking me to protest with all my might against this line; Radville does not want it. I have not beard one elector say one word in favour of this proposed line; I did not hear about it at all until I came to Ottawa, and I do not think anybody is asking for it except a few men in the city of Regina. It has been said that where there is no actual necessity for a railway no work Should be done, and I heartily agree with that. I would ask the members to do all they can to stop this project right here and now.

I am mot acquainted
with the location, of this road or of the necessity for it, but I cannot help thinking it is rather unfair that members who have railroads in their own constituencies Should discuss this matter in this way when the member for Regina (Mr. Motherwell) is not in the House. I imagine he is interested in it. I am only making the suggestion to the minister that it might be well. for the committee to rise and report progress so that the matter can be taken up again when the member for Regina is in his place.

speechtext: Is the hon. member not assuming too much? The Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Motherwell) usually claims he is against the rest of the government.

I have had quite a number

Oh, oh.

would point out that so far as coal is concerned it travels from Swift Current down to Moose Jaiw, to Avonlea, to Gravelbourg and to Neidpath-all the way round that district, a distance of nearly three hundred miles, whereas the district might be served by our Canadian National Railways running into Swift Current, a distance of twenty-five miles. speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext:
Perhaps before we go
into committee the Minister might inform the House whether the government is serious about this resolution; or is it only a try out, too?

speakerposition: Minister of Railways and Canals
speechtext:
This bill, like others, is a serious recommendation. The conditions of the other line were somewhat peculiar. I did not dream that nobody in the House wanted it. It was recommended in accordance with an agreement made by the Canadian National Railways with the city of Regina which agreement stated that the Canadian National Railway Company would give it reasonable support; and I submit that in recommending it they kept their contract.
Motion agreed to and the House went into committee, Mr. Gordon in the chair.

I wonder if the minister in connection with this line would give us a statement as to railway policy. We had this matter u,p two years aigo and again last year. There was a project very much favoured by the people of the district of extending the line from Bengouigh west. It was to run west, almost parallel, perhaps branching off a little to the southern boundary, a. distance, as I recollect it, of some eighty odd miles, which if constructed would have looked after farmers who are to-day without proper railway connection and at such a distance that they cannot economically haul -grain to railhead. I would like if the minister would explain the present construction, which appears to be deflected somewhat to the north and away from the district that really requires it. I am not saying that some people may not be helped here, -but I Would hope that helping them is not going to defeat the hopes of those to the south, which are of very, very long standing.
fMr. Graham.]

speakerposition: Minister of Railways and Canals
speechtext: As my hon. friend knows, there was a good deal of discussion in the committee last year over what was called the Radville line, and I think there has been contention over it for a good many years. The original project of the Canadian Northern was to build the branch as outlined in this bill, but last year a change was made to cover a greater amount of territory, the line to run in a direction more southerly, if I relmember the map correctly. The question arose in the committee last year that part of this territory might better be supplied by the Canadian Pacific. Now the committee and parliament have been expressing more and more every year the desirability of lessening the overlapping in railway construction by the two lines, and the Canadian Pacific has agreed, I understand1, in fact, I have seen a letter to that effect, to construct a .line to take care of the large part of the territory the Canadian National Railway was proposing to take care of in its last year's construction.
Which construction, Radville or Bengough?

speakerposition: Minister of Railways and Canals
speechtext: Radville.

I do not think
anyone will look after that.

speakerposition: Minister of Railways and Canals
speechtext:
It is in that direction, although I will not say it goes to Radville itself. I will read .the memorandum on the Bengough-Willowbuneh line:
It is proposed in 1925 to let a contract for the grading of the 27 miles to be completed in that year at an estimated cost of $500,000. In 1926, the track-laying and ballasting will be done and the line generally completed to Willowbuneh at an estimated cost for that year of $445,000.
I may say the distance is 27 miles:
This line replaces the Radville S. & W.,-a bill for which was turned down in the Senate last year. During

C.N.R.-Branch Lines
the discussion on the bill last year, it was suggested that if the Canadian Pacific Railway would build eastward into the Fife Lake territory, the Canadian National Railways would be prepared to withdraw from the territory south and west from Radville. Now the Canadian Pacific Railway is prepared to build into the Fife Lake district, not from the east, but from Assiniboia, with the idea of eventually running east from Fife Lake to cross about the territory proposed to be covered by the Radville S. & W. Line, the Canadian National Railways are undertaking their original proposal in that country,-the extension of their Mary-field Branch from Bengough to Willowbunch.
The justification of this line is the fulfilment of undertakings in the past to construct this line, and also that it will give rail communication to the town of Willowbunch, and shorten the road haul for the farmers in the district south of there.
It is figured the production from the area tributary to the line will be 650,000 bushels of grain on the average per year, besides 170 carloads of freight in and outbound composed of live stock, coal, lumber and merchandise. About ten miles road haul would be saved on the average to the farmers served by this line, and computing this to be worth | cent per bushel per mile on the 650,000 bushels expected from this line, it would mean an annual saving to the farmers of $48,750 for grain haul alone.
Although to build this line, it is estimated will cost $945,000, arrangements have now been made with the Provincial Government of Saskatchewan to consent to the release of $400,000 of trust funds, which had been previously raised for the purpose of construction of lines in the Province of Saskatchewan. This makes the amount to be voted by parliament $545,000.
I think that is about in line with what I said at the beginning. I do not know how it will strike parliament, but dt struck me as a very good solution if the Canadian Pacific would look after that territory and eventually lead to practically the same territory as would have been covered by the Canadian National branch in last year's programme. The Canadian Pacific would not build down into that territory if the Canadian National built, so the Canadian National has returned to its original proposal to build from Bengough to Willowbunch, and the Canadian Pacific is to build easterly as indicated.

Will the minister say
that there is an arrangement at the present time between the Canadian Pacific and the Canadian National with regard to the development of railway facilities in that country? Does he know there is such an understanding?

speakerposition: Minister of Railways and Canals
speechtext:
I may say that I read
a letter from Mr. Grant Hall outlining just what I have intimated to the House, showing that they propose this year to begin construction.
Have they existing statutory powers to construct in that territory? *

I think before we proceed with this line of railway from Bengough
we are entitled to full information with regard to the Radville line. The Radville line a year ago involved an expenditure of $3,800,000 odd of the money of the tax-10 p.m. payers of this country. At the time that proposition was before this House I opposed it on the ground that the line from Radville south and west was not a feasible proposition, and as a result of the opposition offered in this chamber the bill was amended so that the Canadian National management would have authority to build a road either from Radville, Ritchie or Bengough. I submitted then, and I submit now, that the Canadian National Railway, or their board of engineers at all events, knew at that time that the railway should have been built in the first place from Bengough south and west in the district of Fife lake and Wood mountain. They had that information, but for some reason the road was projected from Radville. Following the rejection of the bill by the Senate the Canadian National engineers were sent into that district, and they were surveying the Radville territory as recently as January last, according to the information I have. I believe they went on the ground some time after harvest, in the fall of last year, and made a survey of the Radville line as proposed before this House last year. Now what I want to know and what I think the country is entitled to know, is what was the result of the information w'hich they procured when they made a survey of that line. I do not know if the minister has it in his possession at the present time, but I think the House and the country are entitled to that information. These people through that south country have suffered tremendously for many years because of their inability to secure a railway, and while the district south of Radville does contain an area where the people are a long way from the railway, that area is comparatively small. The difficulty with the Radville line was that it penetrated forty or fifty miles or more of a country which did not warrant the building of a railway. If the line had been built from Bengough, as proposed two years ago in this House, south and west to Fife lake, and then extended to as far as range 7 or 8 or 9, west of the third meridian, there is no other branch of the Canadian National which could serve a better country or one better calculated to develop railway tonnage. That country between what is known as Big Muddy through Fife lake country and clear through to White Mud river, is a country where there has been scarcely a crop failure since the settlers first went in there. I do
C.N.R.-Branch Lines

not live there myself, but I know it well. It is better than the district I live in. In 1910 when there was a general crop failure throughout southwestern Saskatchewan, in the region know as Summer Cove there was an average yield of grain running from twenty to thirty bushels to the acre. Mixed farming is carried on throughout the Fife lake and Wood mountain country which is different from the area west of the White Mud river. Would the hon. gentleman tell us what information he has with regard to the report of the engineers whom the National Railway had on the ground last fall and winter?

speakerposition: Minister of Railways and Canals
speechtext: The hon. gentleman knows that these engineers never come to me with reports, unless they are asked for by me. I am not an engineer and do not know anything about the engineering end. I know that the Canadian National board and the Canadian Pacific Railway seemed to arrive at an arrangement which I thought would meet the situation more nearly than any other arrangement which could be made. I would suggest this-and this is why I want to send the bills to-committee-that we proceed with the bill and get it to the Railway committee. Then we could notify the Canadian Pacific Railway and the Canadian National as well. They will be glad to come with their engineers and thresh out the whole matter in detail. There is nothing to hide about it, but this committee and myself are a combination that would not be able to thresh out engineering questions, and there are a hundred questions my hon. friend would like to ask the Canadian Pacific officials. I would like some assurance that this other road is going to be built. My suggestion is that we should get this in the form of a bill, as is done in the case of other bills. If it were a Canadian Pacific Railway bill it would be referred to the Railway committee without discussion. I am not objecting to the discussion, but we could have that discussion much better in the Railway committee than anywhere else.

I do not know if you get my point. I am not offering any opposition to the bill, and I hope that I may not have to offer such opposition, but I want to get a general statement covering a mistake made last year. How did it come that the Canadian National made the mistake last year with regard to the Radville line.

speakerposition: Minister of Railways and Canals
speechtext:
My hon. friend can get
that from the committee.

I think we got that ourselves from the engineers. My hon.

friend will correct me if I am wrong, but as I recollect it, the engineers were called last year in connection with the Radville line, and they said they had always reported against it. They said it could not be built and would be a waste of money.

speakerposition: Minister of Railways and Canals
speechtext: They did not say that in my presence.

That is the
evidence on oath before the Senate, but they were talking for themselves and not for anybody else.

My hon. friend from
West York is quite correct. I heard the statement made by the engineering department of the Canadian National, and those witnesses, not only before the- Commons committee, but before the Senate committee, intimated that so far as. the railway companies were concerned, they had always advocated the construction of the line from Ben-gough rather than from anywhere else.

We are only
now considering a resolution. The matter will have to come before the House in com-

C.N.R.-Branch Lines
raittee in connection with a bill, and I have no doubt the minister will come before us with all the information. The information we would really like would be an assurance that no further attempt will be made to throw away money south of Radville in that Big Muddy river district in the manner described, and that instead of having lines built which are more in the nature of political fences than anything else, we will have lines built for the farmer. If the minister comes down and assures the House that there is no more danger of that Radville proposition being attempted to be put through I think the resolution might pass.

I do not think we
should let this resolution go through too hastily. I want first to assure the minister that, coming from the district which this resolution directly affects, I have great pleasure in giving it my full support. I know the situation well, and I am glad to see the minister is taking a step to meet the difficult situation which we have there. One suggestion, however, that I have to make in connection with this resolution-and I recommend it to the minister's consideration-is that, instead of having this legislation apply only to lands south of township 16, it should apply to the entire area as far north as the South Saskatehawan river. The situation is the same and the river would be a natural boundary. To make an arbitrary arrangement that there should be a difference with regard to the working out of the Dominion Lands Act as between north and south of township 16, will create a situation whereby many perplexities will be bound to arise. For example, supposing when this measure becomes law, a resident living in township 16 or 17, desires to make entry for a parcel of land in township 15, what will the situation be? Will he have a right to make entry? As the situation with regard to climate and soil in connection with abandoned lands south of the Saskatchewan river is practically the same, I would recommend very earnestly that this legislation be made to apply as far north as the South Saskatchewan river.
C.N.R.-Branch Lines

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
This is a
departure from the strict principle that applies to homesteading, inasmuch as we are first giving a preference to applications of residents over those of people living outside of the territory. This has never been done before. Personally I am very anxious to prevent homesteading in those areas, but there are some circumstances in which sons of residents in the locality can advantageously be settled' on some of those lands and permitted to carry on agricultural! pursuits. I think my hon. friend will agree with me that it will be well to discourage as far as possible the carrying on of agricultural pursuits, because most of the people there have turned their attention almost altogether to ranching. I am speaking of the area where this legislation will apply particularly and I do not want to extend this privilege over too great an area. I quite foresee the difficulty my hon. friend has pointed out, that some one, for example living in the township just north, might be deprived of the privilege, but I would like to see what sort of an onslaught is going to be made on us for opening up some of those lands. I confess I am not friendly to encouraging agriculture in that area, because we know it is the dry area, and we are rather attempting to encourage ranching, a system of agriculture that we know will be successful there. But we think it is a hardship to deprive a young man coming of age of the privilege of a free homestead if it is available and if, in our opinion, after investigation, there is a reasonable chance of success. That is all we are putting this clause in for.

I do not want to hold up this bill, or to enter into a long dissertation upon it, but I want at this time to correct a misapprehension on the part of this House and the people of this country regarding that area. An arbitrary ruling was made, I think in 1921, with regard to the regulations of the Dominion Lands Act by setting aside as area A all lands in southern and western Saskatchewan south of township 16. Under that ruling those lands have been blacklisted. That area is known as the blacklist, as area A under the Dominion Lands Act. What are the facts with regard to that area? I live in it myself, in township 12, where a heavier tonnage of agricultural products is raised than in any other area of Saskatchewan. I make that statement without fear of contradiction. It is not true that the country is not fit for agriculture. It is one of the best districts in Saskatchewan or Alberta, but it has a feature which hon. 	I
members and the public at large do not understand. I have explained it several times before and I am going to explain it again for the benefit of hon. members. The land in Manitoba and eastern Saskatchewan is uniform. It is a heavy clay soil that is very general. When you get to a few miles west of Weybum, what is known as the Missouri plateau, you reach a different class of land entirely. You have a class of land which is broken, where you have large areas of first class soil, large areas of medium class soil and large areas of the poorest kind of soil, areas that are fit only for grazing purposes. Consequently you see, Mr. Chairman, the hardship it is on residents of those large good areas to have their land classed and put down as being unfit for agriculture, when that argument applies only to those areas that are sandy and, of course, fit only for grazing.
In regard to the point involved here, I have objected time and again to that arbitrary ruling setting aside the line south of township 16, because for a considerable distance south of the South Saskatchewan river the quality of the soil and the climate are practically the same. There is no justification for making township 16 the dividing line as between one class of these lands and another, and that is one of the reasons why I wish to bring this matter to the attention of the minister. If he is going to give countenance in legislation again to the belief that there is a difference between the land south of 16 and the land to the north he will simply create a blacklist against the land in the south country. I do not know whether the minister is familiar with the country, but I venture to suggest that in that area between what is known as the Cypress hills and Maple Creek, to the town of Assiniboia, which includes a district of approximately 50 or 60 miles wide and covers 100 miles long, there is some of the very best agricultural land in the west; there is no area in all western Canada that has developed more agricultural products in the last twelve years. All that area is south of township 16, and that is the regrettable feature of this proposal. There are many immigrants coming into the country to-day from the United States for the purpose of settling on farm land and when they make inquiries they will be told not to go into that country because it is the dried out section, to use the term which the minister has employed. But it is no such thing. It is true that there are parts of that country that are dried out, but they do not lie mainly south of township 16; as a matter of fact, most of the dried out areas are north of it.

C.NJR.-Branch Lines
Let me refer to one. Anyone going through on the main line of railway between Swift Current and the Alberta line will pass along a sandy or bad area north of that line, not far from where I live. Again south of the Cypress hills, between them and the American boundary, there is an area that can be described as dried out, where it was a mistake in the first place for people to settle. In fact, close to my own town there is a considerable area that should not have been settled at all. But my point is that to make township 16 the dividing line between what is considered as good land and what is considered the dried out section is simply to leave a blacklist on that country south of township 16, and that is a rank injustice to the people who are trying to make that part of the country profitable.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
I quite
agree with my hon. friend (Mr. McTaggart) that some of the finest land in western Canada lies in that area; and I might include the area directly south of Swift Current along the boundary line. There is a portion in southern Alberta, not far from the boundary of the Saskatchewan, which is very fertile. But generally speaking the best of these lands are already homesteads. I believe that the area my hon. friend mentions is almost without exception all given over to homesteads as far west as Assiniboia. Now. I am not suggesting a black List of the territory. What we propose under the amendment, as my hon. friend will realize, is that in some of those areas where we have application for opening up homesteads in what we consider to be lands unfitted for that purpose, such lands should be dealt with in a particular way. We do not want to blacklist any lands; but there are frequently alongside some of these ranches fairly desirable quarter sections suitable for farming purposes and we are simiply asking the right to deal with these particular cases and to trea/t the sons of residents of the locality as preferred settlers. That is all we are doing. Township 16 has of course been fixed upon more or less as an arbitrary boundary, but we are merely experimenting in that regard. To 'be frank, I am afraid that we shall have a considerable demand for land's where I do not think that settlement should be permitted. However, we are trying this out to see how it will work.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: When was the blacklisting done?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
There is no such thing as a blacklisting, but in 1921 it
was decided not to permit more homesteading in certain areas.

Any abuse of the privilege of opening up land south of 16 can be overcome by the inspectors making a proper report to the department. If, in their opinion any land is not fit for farming purposes they can refuse to allow it to be homesteaded. But there are men living there who cannot sell out to-day, and as their boys are coming of age, and they are unable to keep them at home, it is desirable that they should be able to obtain land adjacent to the homestead for their boys. In that case, they do not need to put up buildings, and while the land would not be worth while to an outsider, who would be free to go anywhere he liked, it is certainly of value to those who are resident in the locality and who cannot move. There is not much inducement for the outsider to come in but undoubtedly the resident who is stuck there and cannot sell out can utilize the land adjacent to his farm. The outsider of course can go north where there are lots of good homesteads. This move on the part of the government is a good one, and will, I think, bring a good deal of satisfaction to the residents of that south country.

I want to commend this
move which the minister is making and which I think is a very proper one. I believe that the sons of the people who have pioneered that country should have the first choice of any homesteads that are available. I would suggest to the minister however that he is making the area, to which he is applying this scheme, altogether too small. There are many areas in Alberta where the scheme should be put into operation. There are a great many young men coming of age and there are no homesteads available to them unless they go several-hundred miles north; and it is rather a hardship, after these old pioneers have gone into that country and established a community, suffering all the hardships which pioneers have to endure, to see the few homesteads that are left picked up by outsiders. I suggest that along the foot hills west of Claresholm there are a number of families who in some cases have one or two sons that are old enough to establish homesteads and who might be given an opportunity to take up these lands. The land along there is nearly all held under lease but a few quarter sections have been released and they do not always go to residents in the vicinity. The scheme which is outlined in this resolution is a splendid one, but I would advise the minister to enlarge the area to which it should apply. I think we have
Annuities Act

been altogether too free in disposing of homestead lands to Doukhobors, Galicians and people of other nationalities who it is doubtful would be an asset; more likely they are a liability to the country. It will be only a few years before our young men will be looking for free lands and there will not be any good homesteads left for them within a reasonable distance of the railway. I think the minister should go a good deal further in this bill and apply the scheme to considerable areas in Alberta and Saskatchewan. I think it is only right that what free lands are left there should be reserved for the people who have pioneered that country.
Resolution reported, read the second, time and concurred in. Mr. Stewarlt thereupon moved for leave to introduce Bill No. 75 to amend the Dominion Lands Act.
Motion agreed to and bill read the first time.

Hon. ERNEST LAPOINTE (Minister of Justice) moved the second reading of Bill No. 43, to amend the act to authorize rearrangements and transfers of duties in the public service.
Motion agreed to, bill read the second time, and the House went into committee thereon, Mr. Gordon in the chair.
On section 1-Duties and powers of minister and department to be exercised by minister and department to which transfer of duties is made.
Would the minister kindly explain the bill?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
Under chapter 67 of the Revised Statutes concerning the Department of Agriculture, it is provided that the duties of the minister with regard to certain matters under his control may be transferred to some other department or branch of the civil service, and that the management of any one of those matters so transferred shall go to another minister of the crown, and such minister is substituted with all the powers and duties of the Minister of Agriculture. An act was passed in 1918 to authorize rearrangements and transfers of duties for all departments in the public service. Under this act, the powers, duties and functions of any minister of the crown may be transferred to another minister, or from one department to another, or from one branch of the service to another. Now the commission which is considering the revision of the statutes has suggested this amendment, which will make the

Public Service Rearrangement
provision in the Department of Agriculture Act general for all departments. The amendment will remove any doubt as to the transfer of such duties. It is merely a formal matter.

If the minister wished to
simplify the work of his department through the transfer of a particular branch of it to the Department of the Secretary of State, for instance, then this bill would permit that transfer and vest in the Secretary of State the authority over the branch so transferred; is that the idea?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: Yes. The power already existed under the act of 1918, but this makes it quite clear that the duties in question are automatically transferred, in the case my hon. friend mentions, to the Secretary of State.
Would that be a permanent transfer?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
Until the Governor in
Council changed it again, if he chose to do so.

I received a letter the
other day, I have forgotten from whom, protesting very strongly against this measure and implying that there was "a nigger in the woodpile," as the expression is. I do not know where the nigger is myself, and the Minister of Justice does not know either, I hope.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
I assure my hon. friend
it is entirely a "white" deal.
Then we have the assurance of the minister that it is merely to simplify the procedure?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: It does not even change the law. It simply makes it clearer and more uniform.

Has the transfer of
branches from one department to another been very frequent?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
No. It was done a
good deal during the war, because of the arduous work that some ministers had to do. Of late it has seldom been done.

Under this law could a
branch be transferred from the outside service to the inside service?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: I suppose it could.

I .think the minister is right- in saying that during the war orders in council were passed making transfers of certain rights and duties for the purpose of expediting business. I do not remember
of the powers under the 1918 act being exercised in any other way. But how would the employees be affected if a branch outside were brought inside to a department which looked upon the activities of the outside branch as entirely unnecessary? Would the duties of those employees so transferred simply lapse? If so, it would be an opportunity for the appointment of a whole lot of other officials. Has this whole question of employment been considered in this connection?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
This bill makes it clear that the only thing that is changed is the control of the branch by one minister instead of another, and its being in one department instead of another. Everything else remains the same. The present act reads as follows:
1. (1) The Governor in Council shall have power,-*
(a)	to transfer any powers, duties or functions or the control or supervision of any part of the public service from one minister of the crown to any other minister of the crown, or from one department or portion of the public service to any other department or portion of the public service; or,
(b)	to amalgamate and combine any two or more departments under one minister of the crown and under one deputy minister.
So 'that the employees are raither protected by the amendment, because it is made clear that nothing is changed except the head of the department or of the branch. I have pointed out that the change was suggested by the commissioners who are studying the revision of the statutes. The wording is borrowed from the Department of Agriculture Act, chapter 67 of the Revised Statutes, and the provision is made applicable to all departments.

The real effect of that section in the act of 1918 would seem to be to make it clear that the minister or the department to whom the branch was transferred would in law have those powers; that the original power is in no way lost by the transfer. But my point was with regard to transfers from the inside to the outside service, or vice versa.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
That is not mentioned
either in the act as it exists to-day or in this amendment.

I am not sure
but that it should be mentioned. However, I understand the minister to assure us that any transfer under this bill will not in any way affect the standing of those in the civil service.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
I am giving that assurance to my hon. friend.
Migratory Birds Act

That is quite
sufficient for me. I had hoped that there was something else behind the bill-that there was to be a combining of departments to cut down expenses. If my hon. friend would say that was the real reason of it, we would all say, Amen.
