stagedirection
speechtext:
Hon. CHARLES STEWART (Minister of the Interior) moved the second reading of Bill No. 44, to amend the Migratory Birds Convention Act.
Motion agreed to, bill read the second ;ime, and the House went into committee thereon, Mr. Gordon in the chair.
On section 1-Regulation as to possession of birds.
Will the minister explain?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
Certain
court decisions have made it appear that the present act and regulations forbid the possession of migratory birds legally taken in open season at any other time than in open season. That is, if one shoots game birds during the open season, and then has them in his possession after the open season closes, he is liable to prosecution. I am curing that by making the regulations conform with those in vogue in the provinces.

How is that
going to work out? We have no period stated in the bill. I suppose the minister's idea is to bring in regulations providing how many weeks or days.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
My idea is that the regulations will conform with the provisions of the provincial game acts. They vary somewhat in the different provinces, but 
we will arrange it so that there will be no confusion.
If we pass paragraph (aaa) I suppose the regulations, which will be made by the Governor in Council, will provide the period which each province provides by statute.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: Yes.
Would the minister explain just how we have concurrent jurisdiction here and the necessity for concurrent legal action?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: This amendment is necessary because of the fact that prosecutions have taken place in the province of Manitoba where the birds shot legally in open season were held until after the close of the season, which was 'permissible under the provisions of the provincial act, but not permissible under our act. In order that there shall be no confusion in the minds of those responsible in the various provinces, we are providing regulations for the keeping of game the same as those prevailing in the provinces.

I confess I am
not familiar with the present method of administration of game laws. I have not followed it this last few years, but is there any conflict at all between the local and the Dominion enforcement of law? How is it arranged? It used to be arranged, as I recollect it, by the local authorities looking after the enforcement of the law through their local game keepers and the like, or through local police officers. W'hat do we do about it? Are we now employing a number of men to see that people do not shoot birds out of season?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
Yes, to
some extent, but my hon. friend will notice that by the next section we are making an arrangement with Ontario, which is practically the last province, to utilize their
11 p.m. game officers in the enforcement of the law. We have very few men, and they are mostly in eastern provinces, very few all told, who are enforcing the Migratory Birds Convention Act. The desire is to utilize the game officials of the provinces.

I would like
to ask the Minister of Justice as to what in his view is the underlying jurisdiction in connection with the enforcement of game laws, whether it is provincial or whether it is Dominion.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
I will be pleased to look into the question and answer my hon. friend.

Migratory Birds Act
I would not venture to give an opinion on it to-night.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
The federal
authorities have the responsibility of enforcing the Migratory Birds Act, because it is based upon a treaty with our American neighbours, but our desire is to utilize the provincial officials who are engaged in this work, and the arrangement provided by the next section covers the Ontario officials.

I suppose the
effect of what my hon. friend says is this, that so far as the Migratory Birds Act, which, of course, is something we have in common with the United States, is concerned, the regulations adopted under it have been made by the government. to conform to the different open seasons in the provinces. Am I right in that?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: Yes, practically so. There may be some slight differences. Our regulations may not conform in all cases exactly with the regulations of the provinces as to open season, and so on, but there could be no shooting of migratory birds under the provincial acts because the federal authorities are responsible for the enforcement of the act in its entirety.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
Of course, there is a
treaty in connection with this matter, and that makes it a matter of federal jurisdiction under the British North America Act. Section 132 of the British North America Act provides:
The parliament and government of Canada shall have all powers necessary or proper for performing the obligations of Canada or for any province thereof, as part of the British Empire, towards foreign countries arising under treaties between the empire and such foreign countries.
So as there is a treaty, we have the right to deal with it.

Did I understand the
Minister of the Interior to say that the Dominion government has the right to make regulations as to open season?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
So far as the migratory birds are concerned.
Mr. MANIiON: But not in regard to others?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: No.
What game birds have we got that are not migratory?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: A great number, quail, partridge, prairie chicken, to mention only a few. Over these the provinces have jurisdiction.

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext:
Section agreed to.
On section 2-provincial officers to be game officers, except as to moiety of fines.

What is the
reference to subsection 2 of section 12 which "shall not apply to any such officers"?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
That is so
far as payment of moiety of fines is concerned. This section is simply to provide that the Ontario game officers shall be officers for the enforcement of this act.

Will	the federal
department be responsible for any expenses? There have been disputes in the past over expenses.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
Oh yes, we
have to be responsible for expenses in connection with the enforcement of the act.
M,r. ROSS (Kingston):	Will	that apply
just from the passing of this amendment or to the past as well? There have been several cases in dispute.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: If my hon. friend refers to Ontario, we have an arrangement for the settlement of past disputes. This arrangement was made when giving authority to these officers to carry out their duties, I cannot give my hon. friend the particular instances, but we have had1 a full discussion and a full understanding with the department in Ontario.

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext:
Section agreed to.
On section 3-No one to buy, sell or possess bird, nest or egg during prohibited time.
It looks as if this section were rendered necessary by the previous amendment.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: Yes.
Are there not special privileges or lioemse given to certain individuals to have in their possesion these eggs and so on?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
Yes, there
are certain individuals who are collecting for different purposes, but they must get permission or license. There are certain officers who give these privileges to collectors, and they are always given with the approval of the chief migratory bird officers. The permission comes through the local officials, but. the permission is passed upon by the chief officer: In most cases they are persons of some note, and the officers do not grant these licenses indiscriminately. Scientists are given this permission
Dairy Produce Act

to collect for museum and university purposes and so on.

speechtext:
Section agreed to.

speakerposition: topic
stagedirection
speechtext:
Hon. W. R. MOTHERWELL (Minister of Agriculture) moved the second reading of Bill No. 72, to amend the Dairy Produce Act.
Motion agreed to, bill read the second time, and the House went into committee thereon, Mr. Gordon in the chair.
On section 1-Regulations.
Explain.

speakerposition: Minister of Agriculture
speechtext:
While this bill is
not very long, it is very important. The purpose of the bill is to refuse the grading privileges to anybody who persists in the adulteration of either butter or cheese. We have had one case referred back from Great Britain where butter has been found to be adulterated with various oils, and when we bring it home to the culprit, he sometimes pays a fine; but proceeds to repeat the offence, feeling that he can make more money by paying the fine and continuing to commit the offence than to refrain from doing it. The most effective way is to refuse to grade the product of those who are guilty of the offence; then, they cannot export their produce. By that means you protect your butter and your cheese from being adulterated and sent abroad, because these adulterations destroy our market. We are making a practice of doing this at the present time, -but it is not quite clear that we have the authority to refuse to grade. Therefore we want to amend the act to make it clear that we have the right to refuse to grade butter or cheese in the case of persistent adulteration. I think the provision will be very effective. If anybody challenged our right now we might 'have difficulty in proving that we have the right.

The hon. minister says one thing and the statute says another. He wants the power to refuse to grade dairy produce in the case of obstinate people who will not comply with his regulations. That limitation is not in the bill. There is no limitation here at all.

speakerposition: Minister of Agriculture
speechtext: No.

The minister is taking the right to refuse to grade anybody's dairy products, and withholding the grading certificates from anybody whenever he pleases.

I should have thought, when dealing with a statute in as important a matter as this, the statute should make it clear in what particular kind of cases the department should take that extraordinary power. It seems to me this matter has not been properly considered or drafted. Surely we do not want something on the statute book of Canada that is going to give any minister the right, without the slightest cause being shown, of refusing to grade dairy products and withholding grade certificates. The statute should show why that is being done. It should show that it is to cover the case of people who are not treating their dairy product properly and are hurting the trade. It should not 'be left in that position when it could be made right in a very few minutes, if anyone would take the time to do it.

speakerposition: Minister of Agriculture
speechtext:
If we specified one reason then we could only refuse to grade for that one reason. There may be other reasons besides adulteration. Take a case in point: Out in the west mold in butter has developed, particularly in unsalted butter. We have made careful examination, and we know that some factories get the mold germ, and unless you look after a case of that kind, it is apt to get worse. Some factories persist in shipping moldy butter, and nothing has brought so much distress to the handlers of Canadian products this year as moldy butter. It is just as bad as adulterated butter; as a matter of fact, it is worse, because it develops so rapidly and1 permeates, not only the outside but the entire mass. We have had the worst experience this year since we have started to ship unsalted butter. It seems to me the discretion should be wide enough to apply to moldy butter as well as to adulterated butter, and there may be other things as well. I think the department could have no possible object in refusing a grade unless they were satisfied it was doing positive harm. This power we are taking is nothing like the power taken by Australia, where they absolutely refuse to allow any grade to go out except the top grade. They are jealous of their grades of butter. We are not going that far. We simply want to take authority to refuse to grade. In this bill we specify adulteration as an indication of what the bill is intended to cover, but it is not necessarily confined to adulteration. We could think up everything imaginable in this connection. Foi instance, you might have a persistent offender in the matter of exporting moldy butter, butter in dirty boxes, or butter improperly wrapped in unclean paper. There are a dozen .other things one might think of, but one

Dairy Produce Act
might forget one thing, and if that were not in the bill, we could not put a stop to it without an amendment. That is one of the reasons why we wish to leave the bill as it is. I think the officials of the department may be trusted not to exercise this provision unless they absolutely have to do so. We are exercising it now without the authority, and we think it is better to have a general authority than to have a specific one applied to one offence.

I do not see any reason why it should not be made plain why this should be done. It is not to be done on account of the colour of a man's hair or his eyes; it is to be done because something is wrong with his butter. It is not stated in the bill that it is done because the butter is bad. My point is that it is a question not of saying that you must have good butter-

speakerposition: Minister of Agriculture
speechtext: No.

-but of saying that this departmental action can be used only for the purpose of seeing that people do get good butter. As the bill now stands, what parliament is being invited to do by this government, that always believes so much in democratic ideas and wants to get away from bureaucratic measures but is showing more and more of them than any aggregation we have ever had in this country before, is to give it power to say: We are going to take the right to refuse to grade any farmer's butter we like and we shall not say for what purpose we are going to do that, but for any reason, good, bad or indifferent that appeals to us, we are going to say that that man cannot sell that butter.

speakerposition: Minister of Agriculture
speechtext: He can sell it locally without a grading certificate.
My hon. friend is begging the question entirely. That man cannot under this measure sell his butter in the export market.

speakerposition: Minister of Agriculture
speechtext: That is right.

He is penalized without the slightest thing being said why he should be penalized, without his being told that this is being done in order to assist the production of butter, in order to maintain the standard of Canadian butter, that this is being done because he has moldy butter, rancid butter or anything else. There is nothing of that kind in the bill. Of course, if the government want to legislate in that way, it is for them to say so. It is so easy, if someone
would take just a few minutes time, to cover the cases where this action should be taken. Any legislature that takes the trouble to look after the rights of the individual would see that this was done. Why cannot it be done in this instance?

speakerposition: Minister of Agriculture
speechtext: I will give my hon. friend another instance in regard to which this action should be taken, and that is with regard to cheese. During recent years local factories have followed the practice of shipping cheese almost as soon as it is made to the cold storage plants where it is graded. It is so immature that it is merely a bundle of pressed curd, and it is impossible to do justice to the cheese in that green condition. For instance, supposing a cheese is set somewhere in this neighbourhood and shipped to Montreal a day, or two or three days after it is made, it is just a bundle of curd and it is impossible to do justice to that cheese in the way of grading it when it arrives at Montreal. We want to be able to refuse to grade that cheese for a period at least.. Supposing a shipper wants that graded immediately and put right on the steamer. We cannot grade it immediately and do justice to the cheese. It has to mature for at least ten days before any grader can give justice to it. We want to refuse to grade it until, in our judgment, sufficient time has expired that a reasonably proper grade can be given that the cheese will stand up to. We could specify that too, but this would mean that you would have to have a certain number of these things specified and then you might not catch them all. There is no thought of being arbitrary in this matter. After all, the discretion must lie with the officials of the department as to when they will exercise this authority. As I have pointed out before, this is not a harsh measure, unless some person wilfully wants to go and exercise it an some' brutal or objectionable way, and such an officer should not be in the department to do that. We have to have the bill in this way or to specify everything imaginable that can occur, and I do not think, on short notice, we could catch them all.

I do not want
that done. All I want done is to see that this refers to the question of quality. It does not. There is nothing in this bill referring to standard or quality. The minister is quite right in what he says as regards cheese and I entirely agree with him that cheese ought to be kept for a certain length of time before it is graded for export. The country has been hurt by cheese being shipped that is far too green,
Dairy Produce Act

and the fanners would be away ahead financially if we had some such proper method of ripening cheese as they have on the continent,

speakerposition: Minister of Agriculture
speechtext: We have no authority to do that.

I want to give
the minister authority to do it, but I do not want to give him an omnibus right to do as he pleases with one man and do something different with another.

speakerposition: Minister of Agriculture
speechtext:
We would not do
that.

I aim not at all sure, but what I would like is to be sure that this country's legislation dealing with an important matter of this kind makes it clear that that power-and it is a big and serious power as regards the right of the individual -has to be made use of for a certain purpose, for the purpose of seeing that butter and cheese are being kept up to standard. Nothing of that kind is stated in the bill.

speakerposition: Minister of Agriculture
speechtext: We do not go that far.
My hon. friend, as I recollect his explanation when he introduced this measure, said that he wanted to have these powers in cases of persistent violations of regulations.

speakerposition: Minister of Agriculture
speechtext: That is right.

Why cannot
that be stated?	-

speakerposition: Minister of Agriculture
speechtext: But there are other things like the question of cheese. We are doing this now and there has not been a single objection to it, but you never know when you are going to run across some cantankerous customer who will object just for the fun of it.

I find a good deal
of strong common sense in what the ex-Minister of Finance (Sir Henry Drayton) says and for some reasons in addition to those which he has specified. I believe also it is rather an unhealthy practice to give too much power to any officials without stating the reasons for which the power is given. I would suggest that it would be a comparatively simple matter to state those reasons succinctly, without going into the various cases. So, far as I am aware, there are only two cases why grading certificates should be refused. The first is the unfitness or unsuitability of the product for grading. That would apply to cheese because of its condition. That applies to the product. The

other condition would apply to the individual, and that is a man who consistently violates the provisions of the act. That, to my mind, would practically cover the two cases. I have another reason also, and that is the educative value of letting people know why their stuff was not graded. That educative value is something that should be considered. When an act is passed the people should know why; they should know the reason why their stuff is refused the grading certificate. And when that information spreads throughout the country, when the people know that 'their produce must reach a certain quality and be in a certain condition before the certificate will be granted, there will be a greater impetus to the movement to improve the quality of the goods exported. I think myself that the contention advanced by my hon. friend (Sir Henry Drayton) is a sound one.

speakerposition: Minister of Agriculture
speechtext: In the drafting of a bill you simply state what you want to do and it is not usual to give any explanation as to why ilt is done. The reason for the passing of the law soon gets around. Quite frequently when a new act is passed an explanation accompanies it, especially among new settlers But it is not usual to incorporate such explanations in the act itself.

I am going to make a suggestion to the minister. I suggest that the section should read:
For refusing to grade unfit and unsuitable dairy produce and for withholding grading certificates to any person habituallly disregarding the regulations under this act-
That covers the two points.

speakerposition: Minister of Agriculture
speechtext:
Thalt would be too wide. We might ibake the ground that "unsuitable" included second or third grade butter which although it might not be creditable to the country, would still find a market. But we are not debarring any butter that is wholesome or merchantable from going abroad. We have not gone so far, although they do in Australia and New Zealand. What we have in mind is adulteration, which is a distinct offence. The time may come, when we are neck and neck with New Zealand and Australia, when we shall find it necessary to adopt the same practice and to keep our second and third grade produce at home. At present however we are simply applying the regulation to produce in which there is adulteration or mold, both very objectionable. At present mold is not an offence at all; adulteration is. But the moldy butter may be improved by a little more cleanliness on the part of ithe factory. If some of the

Meat and Canned Foods Act
factories that are turning out moldy butter, and are thus prejudicing the entire butter market of Canada, do not take steps to remedy this evil, there should be some way to bring them to time. But this is not even an offence at the present time; it is simply gross carelessness on the part of the makers, to the detriment of shippers generally. As regards green cheese, there is no offence; there is no law providing that cheese shall be a certain age before it is shipped. A good *many of the factories have not proper storage facilities; they have no cold storage, and with the temperature at 80 or 90 in the shade in the summer, the conditions are not favourable to proper maturing, as they would be with a temperature around 60.

I cannot see that anything would be wider than a law giving the officials absolute power to refuse the certificate for any cause. I quite agree that in the case of such produce as the minister has mentioned the certificate should not be granted to enable exportation. But I do not think that any powers could be wider than those conferred in this act, which is as wide as the universe.

speakerposition: Minister of Agriculture
speechtext: We have to put on these regulations gently.

I move that the section be amended by adding after the word "produce" the words "being unfit or unsuitable for export," and after the word "certificate" the words "to any person habitually disregarding the regulations under this act".

I want to point out an objection that has not yet been raised. The minister is taking the power to refuse to grade dairy produce, and it is suggested that it should be limited to unsuitable dairy produce. How is he to know that it is unsuitable until it is graded? It might be perfectly good butter; the man might have had a change of heart after making one or two bad shipments, and after he had got religion, he might send perfectly good shipments. Is his produce to be rejected simply because he may have happened to make some bad shipments in the past? The amendment is no better, because it takes power to refuse to grade dairy produce that is unsuitable. But how is the minister to know that it is unsuitable until it is graded? I think that we might omit the first part of the provision. The shipper cannot know what his produce is rejected for unless it has been graded. The latter part 184
of the clause, it seems to me, would be ample to meet the object of the minister, which is to prevent the export of inferior butter.

speakerposition: Minister of Agriculture
speechtext:
My intention was
to refer all these bills to the committee on Agriculture, but this one seemed to be so simple, and the explanation I gave appeared to be so complete, that I thought we could dispose of it without referring it to that committee. But if our experts are to disagree probably we shall get a better decision before the committee on Agriculture.
Progress reported.
